I, James Rashad Coleman, Sr., President of the Senate of the State of Colorado, do hereby certify

that, by virtue of the authority vested in me by law, I have prepared for publication, and caused

to be printed, a copy of all the proceedings of the Second Regular Session of the Senate of the

Seventy-Fifth General Assembly of Colorado; that, I have caused to be compared the said printed

Journal with the original manuscript thereof now on file in the office of State Archives, and that

the following is a full, true, and correct copy thereof.


               Dated at Denver, Colorado, this 13 th day of May A.D. 2026.

The text of President Coleman's remarks follow.                                            31
                                                                                           32
Good morning!                                                                              33
                                                                                           34
Welcome to the second regular session of the 75th General Assembly. It is my honor to be 35
with you all this morning to celebrate the beginning of another legislative session.       36
                                                                                           37
I’d like to begin by welcoming our guests this morning. So many family and friends,        38
former lawmakers – basically everyone who doesn’t have to be here when our debates         39
stretch into the night or, god forbid, the weekend.                                        40
                                                                                           41
They aren't here in the chamber today, but I want to acknowledge my family as well. They 42
are my rock, and I would not be here today without them.                                   43
                                                                                           44
Shayna – my wife, and partner of 25 years, thank you for being there to celebrate my       45
successes, for lifting me up on the more challenging days, and for taking on every day     46
together in partnership.                                                                   47
                                                                                           48
Naomi and James – one of the main reasons I do this work is for you. To help build a       49
future where every door is open and every opportunity is waiting for you. My first opening 50
day, you were both small enough to sit on my lap. Flash forward ten years, you’re behind 51
the wheel of a car. I am so proud of both of you and every day you make me grateful to be 52
your dad.                                                                                  53
                                                                                           54
I would like us all to extend thanks to all our nonpartisan staff, who have seen some      55
changes since we were here this summer for our special session. Join me in welcoming our 56
new members of the Senate team, and members taking on new roles on the team:               57
                                                                                           58
Olivia Hart, Mary Ann Admire, Matthew Rivera, Benjamin Noren, Dennis Pinto, and            59
Jerry Touslee.                                                                             60
                                                                                           61
Welcome to the Senate, we’re so happy to have you join the family. And thank you to the 62
returning staff – I’m grateful to work alongside you another year.                         63
                                                                                           64
If you know me, you know that I don’t do any of this alone. I’d like to thank our Senate   65
leadership team – Majority Leader Rodriguez, President Pro Tempore Michaelson Jenet, 66
Assistant Majority Leader Cutter, Caucus Chair Roberts, and our whip, Senator              67
Hinrichsen – for their help in keeping this train on the tracks.                           68
                                                                                           69
I also can’t do this without the greatest Minority Leader this chamber has ever seen,      70
Alamosa’s own, Senator Cleave Simpson. It’s an honor to lead alongside you.                71
                                                                                           72
Page 6   Senate Journal-1st Day-January 14, 2026


         We must also give a warm welcome to the newest member of the upper chamber: Senator              1
         William Lindstedt! Just wait until you see how efficient we are over here.                       2
                                                                                                          3
         I’m just kidding though, of course we love our friends in the House. And I’d be remiss if I 4
         didn’t wish the good Speaker McCluskie well in her final session in the House.                   5
                                                                                                          6
         Her work to invest in Colorado’s future will be transformative. Whether through                  7
         implementation of a new school funding formula that ensures resources are going directly 8
         to students that need them most, her dedication to protecting Colorado’s water future, and 9
         her hand in ensuring access to affordable health care for all – it has been an honor to learn 10
         from her and lead alongside her, and I will miss her partnership.                               11
                                                                                                         12
         Speaker, don’t forget about us on the other side, and please don’t be a stranger!               13
                                                                                                         14
         And to Governor Polis, who is also entering his final year as the leader of our state. It’s     15
         been a privilege to work with you in this leadership capacity and I look forward to all that 16
         we’ll accomplish together this year. I can’t wait to hear your final – and I’m sure best –      17
         State of the State tomorrow. Last year I learned that my assigned seat is fully in view on      18
         the Colorado Channel. I’ve been practicing my facial expressions and reactions all week. 19
         I’m ready!                                                                                      20
                                                                                                         21
         Colleagues, we have been through a lot together over the past year. We have fiercely            22
         debated policies with one another, we have deliberated on Colorado’s toughest issues, we 23
         have celebrated wins.                                                                           24
                                                                                                         25
         And, colleagues, we have grieved together.                                                      26
                                                                                                         27
         We continue to mourn the unexpected, tragic loss of one of our own: Senator Faith               28
         Winter.                                                                                         29
                                                                                                         30
         Faith’s loss is immeasurable, and as we embark on our work this session I hope that we          31
         can incorporate her tenacity and the joy that she found in this work into our policies, as      32
         well as in the conversations we have with one another.                                          33
                                                                                                         34
         Because Faith never forgot to be moved by the people behind her policies. She never             35
         forgot how to be human in this work – flaws and all.                                            36
                                                                                                         37
         She would work with anyone who would work with her. A coalition and team builder for 38
         the ages, she would not let the letter after someone’s name, a district number, or the          39
         county they call home get in the way of getting good policy over the finish line.               40
                                                                                                         41
         Policy that puts Coloradans, and Colorado, first.                                               42
                                                                                                         43
         We will miss her presence in our chamber each and every day. She showed up with a               44
         warmth and brightness reflected in the clothing she wore, the fresh flowers on her desk,        45
         and, most of all, in her smile and friendly hello.                                              46
                                                                                                         47
         May we honor Faith not only in memory, but in how we show up for the work and for one 48
         another.                                                                                        49
                                                                                                         50
         Colleagues, we have accomplished so much together.                                              51
                                                                                                         52
         In just the last year, we stepped up to protect safety net providers through legislation        53
         sponsored by Senators Mullica and Kirkmeyer to ensure Coloradans everywhere from                54
         Craig, Cortez, to Crowley are able to receive the health care they need.                        55
                                                                                                         56
         We set Colorado kids up for greater prosperity by increasing school funding through last 57
         year’s School Finance Act and creation of the Kids Matter Fund, thanks to Senators              58
         Bridges and Kolker.                                                                             59
                                                                                                         60
         We made Colorado a national leader in reproductive rights and we have stood up for a            61
         woman’s right to determine her own future, most recently through passage of legislation 62
         like Senators Gonzales and Weissman’s Emergency Medical Treatment and Labor Act and 63
         Senators Daugherty and Rodriguez’s legislation to implement the will of the voters and          64
         guarantee coverage for abortion care to Coloradans on Medicaid.                                 65
                                                                                                         66
         Over the interim, I had the privilege of visiting every member in their district all across the 67
         state:                                                                                          68
                                                                                                         69
         Senator Rich was kind enough to drive me through District 7 to see the beauty of the            70
         Colorado National Monument and understand the vitality of the Western Slope;                    71
         I traveled up to District 17 to visit Senator Wallace and catch up over a beer at Oskar         72
Senate Journal-1st Day-January 14, 2026                                             Page 7


Blues;                                                                                       1
In District 10, Senator Liston and I toured UCCS and learned about their state-of-the-art    2
cybersecurity systems;                                                                       3
And I joined Senator Roberts at a town hall in District 8 and got to visit Strawberry Hot    4
   Springs.                                                                                  5
                                                                                             6
Not to mention that Minority Leader Simpson and I got to check out some of the coolest       7
cars I’ve ever seen at a car show in Alamosa.                                                8
                                                                                             9
At each of these visits we reflected on our progress and talked about the challenges still  10
facing Coloradans. Colleagues, I’m here to tell you that we are not as divided as some      11
might want you to believe.                                                                  12
                                                                                            13
Coloradans need a safe place to live, they need to be able to go to the doctor without      14
driving for miles or paying a fortune, they need to be able to afford gas, groceries, and   15
childcare. They need clean drinking water and enough water to work the land and grow        16
livestock and crops. And they need us to stand up for their rights and protect their        17
liberties.                                                                                  18
                                                                                            19
To accomplish these goals, we must be courageous leaders and lawmakers.                     20
                                                                                            21
Because we are facing headwinds and will have to confront serious challenges.               22
                                                                                            23
Our budget environment will mean extremely difficult funding decisions. The federal         24
government’s tariffs and haphazard clawbacks of funding for critical programs have sown 25
uncertainty in our economy. They threaten our ability to provide the resources Colorado     26
kids and families, seniors, and rural communities depend on.                                27
                                                                                            28
Colleagues, we are here to work for Colorado, for Coloradans. I know each of us are         29
capable of doing so, because I have seen us do it before. So, I call on each of you to      30
continue to, once again, govern courageously. My great hope is that each of us shows up 31
here ready to work with one another to make life better for Coloradans.                     32
                                                                                            33
We have, and will, work across the aisle to build a better Colorado – because the           34
challenges facing our state demand nothing less.                                            35
                                                                                            36
People across our state are having to stretch their dollars further just to make ends meet. 37
Rent and housing prices are leveling off but remain high. Groceries, insurance, utility     38
bills, and everyday expenses are making monthly budgets a math problem that is              39
increasingly more impossible to solve.                                                      40
                                                                                            41
We have a role to play here. We won’t sit idly by while Coloradans are hurting.             42
                                                                                            43
As we enter Colorado’s 150th year of statehood, we will tackle the big issues head on. Our 44
work this legislative session can and will improve outcomes for Coloradans in every         45
corner of the state.                                                                        46
                                                                                            47
We will build an economy that rewards hardworking people and where every Coloradan 48
has a fair chance to thrive.                                                                49
                                                                                            50
This year we will work to build up affordable housing stock to increase opportunities for 51
homeownership and lower housing prices for everyone. By stabilizing health care             52
premium rates to keep more people on their plans, we can keep insurance premiums            53
manageable for us all. We will continue to take on deceptive pricing practices and hold     54
corporations accountable who pad their pockets at the expense of working families.          55
                                                                                            56
This year, we will also work to streamline workforce programs to help more Coloradans 57
enter highly-skilled careers and fill in-demand positions – strengthening our economy to 58
create more resiliency in the face of turbulent national tides.                             59
                                                                                            60
We’ll follow through on our commitments to reach our climate goals and invest in diverse 61
energy sources to drive down utility costs and bolster an economy that’s ready for our      62
rapidly changing future.                                                                    63
                                                                                            64
We will also govern with the confidence guaranteed to us by our Constitution. Our rights 65
and our freedoms are non-negotiable, and we will find the strength required to do our       66
work knowing that we stand on the right side of history, and on the shoulders of leaders    67
who fought for the freedoms and democracy we enjoy today.                                   68
                                                                                            69
Our work this year will lift us all.                                                        70
                                                                                            71
Now, many of you know I am a minister. I won’t preach too much this morning, but I do 72
Page 8   Senate Journal-1st Day-January 14, 2026


         want to leave you with a few lines of scripture. Matthew 25:                                      1
                                                                                                           2
         For I was hungry and you gave me something to eat, I was thirsty and you gave me                  3
         something to drink, I was a stranger and you invited me in, I needed clothes and you              4
         clothed me, I was sick and you looked after me, I was in prison and you came to visit me.’ 5
                                                                                                           6
         “Then the righteous will answer him, ‘Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or 7
         thirsty and give you something to drink? When did we see you a stranger and invite you            8
         in, or needing clothes and clothe you? When did we see you sick or in prison and go to            9
         visit you?’                                                                                      10
                                                                                                          11
         “The King will reply, ‘Truly I tell you, whatever you did for one of the least of these          12
         brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me.’                                                   13
                                                                                                          14
         Let us work this year for our brothers and sisters who need our help the most. When we           15
         do, we will serve something bigger, greater than each of us in this room. When we do,            16
         we’ll see Colorado’s future in each and every constituent we serve.                              17
                                                                                                          18
         So let us rise to the challenges facing our state and our collective future – as I know that     19
         we can. And let us fill Faith’s shoes and be moved by the work. See each other as equals, 20

         Our work in this building does not end on sine die or when we leave this building, but it 25
         does begin today.                                                                                26

         President Coleman recognized Minority Leader Simpson to address the Senate.                      36

                                                                                                          39
                                                                                                          40
         The text of Minority Leader Simpson's remarks follow.                                            41
                                                                                                          42
                                                                                                          43
         Mister President, members of the Senate, distinguished guests, and the people of                 44
         Colorado:                                                                                        45
                                                                                                          46
         Marriage is a lot like politics. Two people run on bold platforms, make big compromises 47
         during the campaign, and assure everyone they’re committed to reform. Once elected, they 48
         quickly discover there’s a budget crisis, unexpected regulations and far more VETO               49
         power than anticipated. Working together across the aisle becomes essential, transparency 50
         is selective, and success is measured not by getting everything you want, but by keeping         51
         the coalition together long enough to govern.”                                                   52
                                                                                                          53
         As we open the 2026 legislative session, we do so at a remarkable crossroads in                  54
         Colorado’s story. This year marks Colorado’s 150th anniversary of statehood, a milestone 55
         that invites reflection, gratitude, and resolve.                                                 56
                                                                                                          57
         One hundred and fifty years ago, the First General Assembly of the State of Colorado             58
         convened with a Senate made up of just 26 members. They came from mining camps,                  59
         farming communities, frontier towns, and vast rural counties. Among them was Alva                60
         Adams of Rio Grande County (although he represented the House), a man who would                  61
         become one of the youngest Colorado governors at age 36 and whose legacy lives on                62
         today as the namesake of Adams County. That first Senate was smaller in number, but              63
         large in vision. They faced uncertainty, scarce resources, and a rapidly growing                 64
         population, yet they believed Colorado was worth building.                                       65
                                                                                                          66
         That belief did not exist in isolation. It was fueled by enterprise, grit, and institutions that 67
         helped shape our state. This year also marks the 120th anniversary of the National               68
         Western Stock Show, an event that has long celebrated Colorado’s agricultural roots and 69
         the ranchers, farmers, and producers who feed this state and much of the nation. For             70
         generations, the Stock Show has been a meeting place of tradition and innovation, where 71
         heritage is honored, and the future of agriculture is imagined.                                  72
Senate Journal-1st Day-January 14, 2026                                                Page 9


We also recognize the 150th anniversary of the Colorado Mining Association, an               1
organization that played a crucial role in shaping our state. Mining was not just an         2
industry; it was a catalyst. It built towns, funded schools, laid railroads, and drew people 3
from around the world who were willing to risk everything for opportunity. Mining            4
helped turn a territory into a state and a rugged landscape into a thriving economy.         5
                                                                                             6
Behind these institutions were pioneers whose determination still inspires us today. One     7
such pioneer was Otto Mears, often called the “Pathfinder of the San Juans.” Mears           8
understood that prosperity depended on connection, on roads, bridges, and access. When       9
the original copper sheathing of this Capitol dome tarnished under Colorado’s               10
unforgiving weather, it was Otto Mears who convinced the Colorado Mining Association 11
to donate 200 ounces of gold to re-cover the dome. That gold, still shining above us today, 12
is more than decoration; it is a symbol of ingenuity, cooperation, and pride in this state. 13
                                                                                            14
Some of those stories are not just historical footnotes; they are lived experiences passed  15
down through generations. Those roads were challenging, yes, but they connected             16
communities, opened markets, and proved that bold ideas paired with hard work can           17
overcome even the most challenging terrain.                                                 18
                                                                                            19
As we celebrate 150 years of statehood, we honor the men and women who shaped               20
Colorado, beginning with the Indigenous tribes who first stewarded this land and            21
continuing with the diverse generations of Coloradans who brought vision, courage, and a 22
willingness to take risks in pursuit of something better.                                   23
                                                                                            24
While history grounds us, it does not confine us. Colorado’s story has always been one of 25
new horizons, and today, new changes are coming with a new direction.                       26
                                                                                            27
The people of Colorado are clear about what they need from us. They want a state that is 28
affordable, safe, and full of opportunity, but are concerned about how divided we have      29
become. They want a government that listens, that respects their work, and that             30
understands the pressures facing families, small businesses, and communities, urban and 31
rural alike.                                                                                32
                                                                                            33
Our responsibility this session is to chart a roadmap to a new horizon, one that reflects   34
Colorado’s pioneering spirit while responding to today’s realities.                         35
                                                                                            36
At the heart of that roadmap is a simple but urgent priority: lowering costs. Coloradans    37
should not have to work harder just to stand still. Housing costs, energy prices, insurance 38
premiums, and everyday necessities are stretching household budgets across this state.      39
Lowering costs means making responsible decisions with taxpayer dollars. It means           40
scrutinizing spending, reducing unnecessary bureaucracy, and recognizing that every         41
policy choice we make has real consequences for real people. Government should be a         42
partner in affordability, not an obstacle to it.                                            43
                                                                                            44
Lowering costs also requires us to restore balance between regulation and innovation,       45
between ambition and accountability. Colorado thrives when individuals and businesses       46
are free to create, invest, and grow without excessive barriers. When we get government 47
out of the way, opportunity moves forward.                                                  48
                                                                                            49
Just as important is opening new opportunities for every Coloradan. Opportunity is the      50
reason pioneers crossed mountains, the reason industries took root, and the reason          51
families continue to choose Colorado as their home. Opening opportunities today means 52
ensuring access to good-paying jobs, quality education, and reliable infrastructure. It     53
means supporting workforce training that aligns with the needs of modern industries. It     54
means recognizing that opportunity looks different in Denver than it does in the Eastern    55
Plains, the Western Slope, or the San Luis Valley, and crafting policies that respect those 56
differences.                                                                                57
                                                                                            58
Opportunity also means fostering an economy where innovation is welcomed, where             59
entrepreneurs are encouraged to take risks, and where success is rewarded, not punished. 60
Colorado’s future depends on our ability to attract investment, retain talent, and empower 61
the next generation to build their lives here.                                              62
                                                                                            63
As Leader of the Republican Senate, I stand ready to work with anyone, regardless of        64
party, who is serious about solutions. We will bring forward ideas rooted in freedom,       65
accountability, and respect for the people we serve. We will advocate for policies that     66
empower individuals rather than expand bureaucracy, that encourage work rather than         67
dependency, and that trust communities to know what works best for them.                    68
                                                                                            69
Just as Otto Mears built roads into places others thought unreachable, we must be willing 70
to build pathways into Colorado’s future, paths that may be challenging but that lead to    71
growth, resilience, and shared prosperity.                                                  72
Page 10     Senate Journal-1st Day-January 14, 2026


            Mister President and colleagues, the gold above us on this Capitol reminds us of where we  1
            have been. The work before us will determine where we are going. Let us honor 150 years    2
            of Colorado history not just with words, but with action, by choosing a new horizon        3
            worthy of the next generation.                                                             4
                                                                                                       5
             Thank you, and may this session serve the people of Colorado well.                        6

                                    LETTER OF RESIGNATION                                                  4
                                                                                                           5
           February 10, 2026                                                                               6
                                                                                                           7
           Dear Secretary van Mourik:                                                                      8
                                                                                                           9
           I write this letter to formally submit my resignation as State Senator for Senate District 21, 10
           effective on February 13, 2026 at 5:00 pm. Serving Senate District 21, and formerly            11
           House District 32, has been the honor of a lifetime. I am deeply proud of the work I           12
           accomplished to help lead the Senate Democratic caucus, improve outcomes for                   13
           Colorado’s youth, stand with victims and survivors of violence, and build a better             14
           Colorado for all. I look ahead with gratitude to serving Coloradans in new capacities.         15
                                                                                                          16
              Sincerely,                                                                                  17
              (signed)                                                                                    18
              Dafna Michaelson Jenet                                                                      19
              Senate President Pro Tempore                                                                20

                          "SECTION 4. In Colorado Revised Statutes, 39-2-109, amend (1)(e)            48
                 and (1)(k); and repeal (2) as follows:                                               49
                          39-2-109. Duties, powers, and authority.                                    50
                          (1) It is the duty of the property tax administrator, and the administrator 51
                 shall have and exercise authority:                                                   52
                          (e) To prepare and publish from time to time manuals, appraisal             53
                 procedures, and instructions, after consultation with the advisory committee to      54
                 the property tax administrator and the approval of the state board of                55
                 equalization, concerning methods of appraising and valuing land,                     56
                 improvements, personal property, and mobile homes, and to require their              57
                 utilization by assessors in valuing and assessing taxable property. Said manuals,    58
                 appraisal procedures, and instructions shall MUST be based upon the three            59
                 approaches to appraisal and the procedures set forth in section 39-1-103 (5)(a).     60
                 Such manuals, appraisal procedures, and instructions shall be ARE subject to         61
                 legislative review, the same as rules, pursuant to section 24-4-103 (8)(d).          62
                 Beginning January 1, 2023, the administrator shall comply with subsection (2)        63
                 of this section when modifying the manuals, appraisal procedures, and                64
                 instructions.                                                                        65
                          (k) To prepare and publish guidelines, after consultation with the          66
                 advisory committee to the property tax administrator and approval of the state       67
Senate Journal-36th Day-February 18, 2026                                                Page 189


    board of equalization, concerning the audit and compliance review of oil and                     1
    gas leasehold properties for property tax purposes, which shall MUST be utilized                 2
    by assessors, treasurers, and their agents. Such guidelines shall be ARE subject                 3
    to legislative review, the same as rules, pursuant to section 24-4-103 (8)(d).                   4
    Beginning January 1, 2023, the administrator shall comply with subsection (2)                    5
    of this section when modifying the guidelines.                                                   6
             (2) (a) As used in this subsection (2), "property tax materials" means                  7
    the manuals, appraisal procedures, instructions, and guidelines that the                         8
    administrator prepares and publishes under the authority conferred by                            9
    subsections (1)(e) and (1)(k) of this section.                                                  10
             (b) Prior to proposing any changes to the property tax materials, the                  11
    administrator shall conduct a public hearing described in subsection (2)(d) of                  12
    this section. No less than two weeks prior to the hearing, the administrator shall              13
    publish notice of the proposed changes to the property tax materials. The                       14
    administrator must include in the notice:                                                       15
             (I) The date, time, and place of the hearing; and                                      16
             (II) Either the terms or substance of the proposed change or a                         17
    description of the subjects and issues involved.                                                18
             (c) The administrator shall maintain a list of all persons who request                 19
    notification of proposed changes to the property tax materials. On or before the                20
    date of the publication of notice required by subsection (2)(b) of this section,                21
    the administrator shall provide notice via email of the proposed changes to all                 22
    persons on the list. The administrator shall not charge a fee for sending this                  23
    email notice. Upon request of a person on the list, the administrator may mail                  24
    the notice to the person. Any person on the list who requests to receive a copy                 25
    of the proposed changes by mail must pay a fee to the administrator that is set                 26
    based upon the administrator's actual cost of copying and mailing the proposed                  27
    changes to the person. All fees collected by the administrator are continuously                 28
    appropriated to the administrator solely for the purpose of defraying the cost of               29
    the notice.                                                                                     30
             (d) At the place and time stated in the notice, the administrator shall                31
    hold a public hearing at which the administrator shall afford interested persons                32
    an opportunity to submit written data, views, or arguments and to present the                   33
    same orally unless the administrator deems it unnecessary. The administrator                    34
    shall consider all submissions when finalizing a proposed change to the                         35
    property tax materials that the administrator submits to the advisory committee                 36
    to the property tax administrator for the advisory committee's review in                        37
    accordance with section 39-2-131 (1).                                                           38
             (e) The administrator shall adopt proposed changes to the property tax                 39
    materials consistent with the subject matter as set forth in the notice required                40
    by subsection (2)(b) of this section prior to consideration by the advisory                     41
    committee to the property tax administrator.                                                    42
             (f) Any interested person shall have the right to petition the                         43
    administrator in writing for the issuance, amendment, or repeal of any property                 44
    tax materials. The petition is open to public inspection. The administrator is not              45
    required to take any action based on a petition, but when the administrator                     46
    proposes a change to the property tax materials, the administrator shall consider               47
    all related written petitions.".                                                                48

                         24-70-103. Requisites of legal newspaper.                                    45
                         (1) Any and every legal notice or advertisement shall be published only      46
                 IN THE FOLLOWING ORDER OF PRIORITY in a daily, a triweekly, a semiweekly, or         47
                 a weekly newspaper of general circulation: and printed or published in whole         48
                 or in part in the county in which such notice or advertisement is required to be     49
                 published, except as provided in this section. The newspaper, if published           50
                 triweekly, semiweekly, or weekly, shall have been so published in such county,       51
                 except as provided in this section, continuously and uninterruptedly during the      52
                 period of at least fifty-two consecutive weeks next prior to the first issue thereof 53
                 containing any such notice or advertisement; and the newspaper, if published         54
                 daily, shall have been so published in such county, uninterruptedly and              55
                 continuously, during the period of at least six months next prior to the first issue 56
                 thereof containing any such notice or advertisement. In the case of a                57
                 municipality having territory in two counties, each of which counties has one        58

                 THE LEGAL NOTICE OR ADVERTISEMENT AND THAT SATISFIES THE                             66

                          "SECTION 1. Short title. The short title of this act is the "Promoting    32
                   Responsible End-of-Life Management of Electric Vehicle Batteries Act".           33
                          SECTION 2. In Colorado Revised Statutes, 25-17-1002, amend (2);           34
                   and add (1.5) as follows:                                                        35
                          25-17-1002. Legislative declaration.                                      36
                          (1.5) THE GENERAL ASSEMBLY FURTHER FINDS THAT:                            37
                          (a) ELECTRIC VEHICLES ARE CRUCIAL TOOLS FOR REDUCING                      38
                   GREENHOUSE GAS EMISSIONS, WHICH THE STATE IS STRIVING TO ELIMINATE BY            39
                   2050. ELECTRIC VEHICLES ARE ALSO VITAL TO REDUCING LOCAL AIR POLLUTION           40
                   IN AREAS OF THE STATE, SUCH AS THE DENVER METRO AND NORTH FRONT                  41
                   RANGE AREAS, THAT THE FEDERAL ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY HAS                42
                   DESIGNATED AS BEING IN NONATTAINMENT WITH A NATIONAL AMBIENT AIR                 43
                   QUALITY STANDARD. TO ACHIEVE EMISSION REDUCTIONS NEEDED TO MEET                  44
                   STATE-MANDATED CLIMATE GOALS AND FEDERALLY REQUIRED OZONE LEVELS,                45
                   MANY MORE ELECTRIC VEHICLES WILL NEED TO BE DEPLOYED IN COLORADO.                46
                          (b) AS ELECTRIC VEHICLE SALES IN THE STATE CONTINUE TO GROW,              47
                   SUBSTANTIALLY MORE ELECTRIC VEHICLES WILL BE RETIRED IN THE COMING               48
                   YEARS, AND THEIR BATTERIES, KNOWN AS PROPULSION BATTERIES, WILL NEED             49
                   RESPONSIBLE END-OF-LIFE MANAGEMENT;                                              50
                          (c) PROPULSION BATTERIES OFTEN RETAIN VALUE EVEN AFTER THEY               51
                   CEASE TO POWER THE ORIGINAL VEHICLES INTO WHICH THEY WERE PLACED AND             52
                   CAN BE REUSED, REMANUFACTURED, REPURPOSED, OR RECYCLED. EXTENDING                53
                   THE USEFUL LIFESPAN OF PROPULSION BATTERIES IMPROVES THE                         54
                   SUSTAINABILITY PROFILE OF THE ELECTRIC VEHICLE INDUSTRY AND CREATES              55
                   LOCAL ECONOMIC OPPORTUNITIES.                                                    56
                          (d) MULTIPLE ANALYSES HAVE ESTABLISHED THAT EXPENSIVE AND                 57
                   HAZARDOUS RISKS RESULT FROM THE IMPROPER HANDLING AND DISPOSAL OF                58
                   PROPULSION BATTERIES; AND                                                        59
                          (e) UNWANTED PROPULSION BATTERIES THAT ARE STORED IMPROPERLY              60
                   INSTEAD OF BEING SORTED FOR REUSE, REMANUFACTURING, REPURPOSING, OR              61
                   ULTIMATE RECYCLING AND RECOVERY OF VALUABLE MATERIALS COULD                      62
                   POTENTIALLY REDUCE THE ENVIRONMENTAL BENEFITS OF A ROBUST CIRCULAR               63
                   ECONOMY FOR PROPULSION BATTERIES WHILE ALSO INCREASING THE RISK OF               64
                   BATTERY FIRES. A ROBUST EXTENDED PROVIDER RESPONSIBILITY POLICY IS               65
                   NEEDED TO ENABLE A PROPULSION BATTERY CIRCULAR ECONOMY.                          66
                          (2) The general assembly therefore declares that it is in the public      67
Senate Journal-44th Day-February 26, 2026                                                   Page 259


    interest of Colorado to:                                                                            1
            (a) Require producers of batteries AND PROVIDERS OF PROPULSION                              2
    BATTERIES to finance and implement a coordinated, state-approved system that                        3
    increases access to the safe disposal AND RESPONSIBLE END-OF-LIFE                                   4
    MANAGEMENT of batteries in Colorado;                                                                5
            (b) REDUCE THE INHERENT RISK OF FIRE THAT CAN OCCUR WHEN                                    6
    PROPULSION BATTERIES ARE IMPROPERLY DISPOSED OF; AND                                                7
            (c) ENCOURAGE THE REUSE, REMANUFACTURING, AND REPURPOSING OF                                8
    PROPULSION BATTERIES AND THE ULTIMATE RECYCLING AND RECOVERY OF THE                                 9
    VALUABLE MATERIALS IN A PROPULSION BATTERY THAT CAN BE PUT BACK INTO                               10
    THE SUPPLY CHAIN.                                                                                  11

           (b) (I) ON OR BEFORE JUNE 1, 2030, AND ON OR BEFORE EACH JUNE 1                39
    THEREAFTER, A REPURPOSER SHALL SUBMIT AN ANNUAL REPORT TO THE                         40
    EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR COVERING THE PRECEDING CALENDAR YEAR OF THE                        41
    REPURPOSER'S RESPONSIBLE PROPULSION BATTERY MANAGEMENT. THE REPORT                    42
    MUST INCLUDE THE FOLLOWING:                                                           43
           (A) THE NUMBER OF PROPULSION BATTERIES THAT THE REPURPOSER                     44
    REPURPOSED FROM COLORADO; AND                                                         45
           (B) THE NAME AND ADDRESS OF WHERE THE REPURPOSED BATTERIES                     46
    WERE SOLD OR TRANSFERRED, INCLUDING FOR BATTERIES SENT FOR USE IN A                   47
    SECONDARY APPLICATION AND THOSE SENT FOR PROPULSION BATTERY                           48
    RECYCLING.                                                                            49
           (II) THE ANNUAL REPORT MAY BE UNIQUE TO COLORADO OR MAY                        50
    INCLUDE INFORMATION FOR MULTIPLE STATES.                                              51
           (III) A REPURPOSER THAT IS ALSO A REMANUFACTURER NEED ONLY                     52
    SUBMIT ONE ANNUAL REPORT THAT INCLUDES THE REQUIRED INFORMATION SET                   53
    FORTH IN THIS SECTION.                                                                54
           (11) ON AND AFTER OCTOBER 1, 2028:                                             55
           (a) ALL PROPULSION BATTERIES IN THE STATE MUST BE MANAGED AT                   56
    END OF LIFE IN ACCORDANCE WITH RESPONSIBLE PROPULSION BATTERY                         57
    MANAGEMENT;                                                                           58
           (b) PROPULSION BATTERIES THAT ARE HAZARDOUS WASTE AS DEFINED                   59
    UNDER FEDERAL OR STATE HAZARDOUS OR SOLID WASTE LAWS MUST BE                          60
    MANAGED IN A MANNER CONSISTENT WITH THOSE LAWS;                                       61
           (c) A PERSON SHALL NOT DISPOSE OF A PROPULSION BATTERY BY                      62
    TAKING THE PROPULSION BATTERY TO A LANDFILL; AND                                      63
           (d) A PERSON NOT IDENTIFIED IN THIS SECTION IS RESPONSIBLE FOR                 64
    ENSURING THE RESPONSIBLE PROPULSION BATTERY MANAGEMENT OF                             65
    PROPULSION BATTERIES BY WORKING WITH A SECONDARY HANDLER,                             66
    PROPULSION BATTERY PROVIDER, REMANUFACTURER, REPURPOSER, OR                           67
Page 268       Senate Journal-44th Day-February 26, 2026


                    PROPULSION BATTERY RECYCLER.                                                                 1
                             25-17-1020. Applicability.                                                          2
                             A VEHICLE CONTAINING A PROPULSION BATTERY ORIGINALLY SOLD IN                        3
                    THE STATE IS NOT SUBJECT TO THIS PART 10 WHEN IT IS RETIRED OUT OF STATE.                    4
                             SECTION 7. Act subject to petition - effective date. This act takes                 5
                    effect at 12:01 a.m. on the day following the expiration of the ninety-day period            6
                    after final adjournment of the general assembly (August 12, 2026, if                         7

                    election to be held in November 2026 and, in such case, will take effect on the             12

                        "(1) The office shall contract with the administrator. The office may       30
               select an administrator without a competitive procurement process but shall          31
               announce the contract opening publicly and select the administrator in a             32

               office to support the following programs only:                                       39
                        (a) A land banking program to be administered by the administrator.         40
               The program shall provide grants to local governments and tribal governments         41
               and loans to non-profit organizations with a demonstrated history of providing       42
               affordable housing to acquire and preserve land for the development of               43
               affordable housing. For purposes of this subsection (1)(a), "affordable housing"     44
               means rental housing that has a designated imputed income limit by household         45
               size not to exceed sixty percent of the area median income as established by the     46
               United States Department of Housing and Urban Development and published              47
               by the department or a statewide political subdivision or authority on housing,      48
               and regulated units in the project must have a gross rent limit that does not        49
               exceed thirty percent of the imputed income limitation applicable to the units       50
               and for-sale housing that could be purchased by a household with an annual           51
               income of at or below one hundred TWENTY percent of the area median income.          52
               Mixed use development is an allowable use of land purchased under this               53
               program if the predominant use of the land is affordable housing. Loans made         54
               by the program shall be forgiven if land acquired with the assistance of the         55
               program is properly zoned with an active plan for the development of affordable      56
               housing within 5 years of date the loan is made and if the development is            57
               permitted and funded within 10 years. The lender and borrower may establish          58
               additional terms if needed. If land acquired with the assistance of the program      59
               is not developed within the timeline above, the loan must be repaid, with            60
               interest, as soon as practical, but not more than six months after expiration of     61
               said timeline, unless the office agrees to extend all or a portion of the timeline   62
               in its reasonable discretion. Land acquired with the assistance of the program       63
               that is not developed within the timeline above may be used by the owner for         64
               any purpose upon payment of the loan with interest or, in exchange for a waiver      65
               of interest, conveyed to a state agency or other entity for the development of       66
               affordable housing with the approval of the administrator. All principal and         67

Natural       as follows, and as so amended, be referred to the Committee on Appropriations with             47
Resources     favorable recommendation.                                                                      48
                                                                                                             49
                   Amend printed bill, strike everything below the enacting clause and substitute:           50
                                                                                                             51
                           "SECTION 1. Legislative declaration. (1) The general assembly finds               52
                   that:                                                                                     53
                           (a) The use of second-generation anticoagulant rodenticides, referred to          54
                   as "SGARs", should be restricted to licensed applicators to safeguard public              55
                   health, nontarget wildlife and domestic animals, and the environment;                     56
                           (b) Despite prior proposals and actions by the United States                      57
                   environmental protection agency, SGARs remain widely accessible to the                    58
                   general public;                                                                           59
                           (c) Statistics from America's Poison Centers indicate that children 5             60
                   years old and younger account for 75% of the approximately 3,100 annual                   61
                   human exposures to SGARs reported from 2019 to 2023;                                      62
                           (d) Preventive, permanent, or nonstructure-associated baiting with                63
                   SGARs prolongs the environmental presence of toxic chemicals and increases                64
                   the likelihood of primary and secondary exposure to companion animals and                 65
                   wildlife, including birds of prey and mammalian carnivores;                               66
                           (e) Integrated pest management strategies, which emphasize exclusion,             67
Page 316   Senate Journal-51st Day-March 5, 2026


               proper sanitation, and targeted removal, minimize harm and constitute a                   1
               humane, science-driven, and effective approach to rodent control;                         2
                        (f) In conjunction with using integrated pest management strategies,             3
               limiting the use of SGARs to circumstances that involve documented and                    4
               persistent rodent activity, as verified by means such as electronic rodent                5
               monitoring and as only a "last resort" could reduce unnecessary exposure risks            6
               and cascading household, property, and environmental impacts; and                         7
                        (g) The department of agriculture's broad rule-making authority includes         8
               the authority to adopt rules consistent with state and federal law to further             9
               reduce the unintended exposure to SGARs, including the adoption of rules that            10
               reflect the risk-reduction principles described in this section.                         11
                        (2) The general assembly therefore declares that restricting the use of         12
               SGARs, while promoting integrated pest management strategies and                         13
               encouraging the targeted, structure-associated use of SGARs, will protect                14

                       (II) AN INSTITUTION OF HIGHER EDUCATION MAY CONDUCT THE STEPS      11
               LISTED IN SUBSECTION (5)(d)(I) OF THIS SECTION SIMULTANEOUSLY IF THE       12
               INSTITUTION DEEMS IT NECESSARY.                                            13
                       (III) THIS SUBSECTION (5)(d) DOES NOT PREVENT AN INSTITUTION OF    14
               HIGHER EDUCATION FROM ESTABLISHING ADDITIONAL PRELIMINARY WELLNESS         15
               ASSESSMENT STEPS. THE DEPARTMENT OF HIGHER EDUCATION MAY ADOPT             16
               RULES TO ESTABLISH ADDITIONAL PRELIMINARY WELLNESS ASSESSMENT STEPS.       17
                       (IV) (A) AN INSTITUTION OF HIGHER EDUCATION IS NOT DEEMED TO       18
               HAVE FAILED TO CONDUCT A PRELIMINARY WELLNESS ASSESSMENT SOLELY            19
               BECAUSE, DUE TO CIRCUMSTANCES BEYOND THE INSTITUTION'S REASONABLE          20
               CONTROL, ONE OR MORE OF STEPS OF THE PRELIMINARY WELLNESS ASSESSMENT       21
               COULD NOT BE COMPLETED WITHIN THE SIX-HOUR PERIOD REQUIRED PURSUANT        22
               TO SUBSECTION (5)(b) OF THIS SECTION.                                      23
                       (B) AN INSTITUTION OF HIGHER EDUCATION SHALL DOCUMENT THE          24
               REASON FOR EACH UNCOMPLETED STEP REQUIRED PURSUANT TO SUBSECTION           25
               (5)(f) OF THIS SECTION.                                                    26
                       (e) (I) AN INSTITUTION OF HIGHER EDUCATION SHALL ADOPT AND         27
               PUBLISH A PRELIMINARY WELLNESS ASSESSMENT POLICY THAT DEFINES, AT A        28
               MINIMUM:                                                                   29
                       (A) THE CATEGORIES OF INSTITUTIONAL EMPLOYEES OR AGENTS WHO        30
               ARE AUTHORIZED TO CONDUCT A RESIDENTIAL VERIFICATION PURSUANT TO           31
               SUBSECTION (5)(d)(I)(B) OF THIS SECTION, WHICH MUST INCLUDE AT LEAST ONE   32
               CATEGORY OF EMPLOYEE OR AGENT AVAILABLE OUTSIDE OF REGULAR BUSINESS        33
               HOURS;                                                                     34
                       (B) THE INSTITUTION OF HIGHER EDUCATION'S PROCESS FOR              35
               ESCALATING A MISSING PERSON REPORT TO AN EMPLOYEE RESPONSIBLE FOR          36
               INITIATING A PRELIMINARY WELLNESS ASSESSMENT;                              37
                       (C) THE INSTITUTION OF HIGHER EDUCATION'S RECORD-KEEPING           38
               SYSTEM REQUIRED PURSUANT TO SUBSECTION (5)(f) OF THIS SECTION; AND         39
                       (D) ADDITIONAL PRELIMINARY WELLNESS ASSESSMENT STEPS AS            40
               ESTABLISHED BY AN INSTITUTION OR ADOPTED BY THE DEPARTMENT OF HIGHER       41
               EDUCATION PURSUANT TO SUBSECTION (5)(d)(III) OF THIS SECTION.              42
                       (II) AN INSTITUTION OF HIGHER EDUCATION SHALL MAKE ITS             43
               PRELIMINARY WELLNESS ASSESSMENT POLICY PUBLICLY AVAILABLE ON THE           44
               INSTITUTION'S WEBSITE AND SHALL REVIEW AND UPDATE THE POLICY AT LEAST      45
               ONCE EVERY THREE YEARS.                                                    46
                       (f) (I) AN INSTITUTION OF HIGHER EDUCATION THAT CONDUCTS A         47
               PRELIMINARY WELLNESS ASSESSMENT PURSUANT TO SUBSECTION (5)(a) OF THIS      48
               SECTION SHALL MAINTAIN CONTEMPORANEOUS WRITTEN DOCUMENTATION OF            49
               THE ASSESSMENT, INCLUDING:                                                 50
                       (A) THE DATE AND TIME THE MISSING PERSON REPORT WAS RECEIVED       51
               AND THE NAME AND ROLE OF THE EMPLOYEE WHO RECEIVED IT;                     52
                       (B) THE DATE, TIME, METHOD, AND OUTCOME OF EACH CONTACT            53
               ATTEMPT MADE PURSUANT TO SUBSECTION (5)(d)(I) OF THIS SECTION;             54
                       (C) THE NAME AND ROLE OF EACH INSTITUTIONAL EMPLOYEE OR AGENT      55
               WHO PARTICIPATED IN THE PRELIMINARY WELLNESS ASSESSMENT;                   56
                       (D) THE REASON ANY STEP OF THE PRELIMINARY WELLNESS                57
               ASSESSMENT WAS NOT COMPLETED WITHIN THE SIX-HOUR PERIOD REQUIRED           58
               PURSUANT TO SUBSECTION (5)(b) OF THIS SECTION, IF APPLICABLE; AND          59
                       (E) THE DATE AND TIME A MISSING PERSON REPORT IS MADE TO THE       60
               INSTITUTION'S POLICE DEPARTMENT OR THE NEAREST LAW ENFORCEMENT             61
               AGENCY.                                                                    62
                       (II) AN INSTITUTION OF HIGHER EDUCATION SHALL RETAIN THE           63
               RECORDS REQUIRED PURSUANT TO THIS SUBSECTION (5)(f) FOR A MINIMUM OF       64
               THREE YEARS AFTER THE MISSING PERSON REPORT WAS RECEIVED BY THE            65
               INSTITUTION OF HIGHER EDUCATION, AND THE RECORDS MUST BE AVAILABLE TO      66
               A LAW ENFORCEMENT AGENCY UPON REQUEST.                                     67
              Senate Journal-51st Day-March 5, 2026                                          Page 323


                          (III) AN INSTITUTION OF HIGHER EDUCATION SHALL MAKE THE RECORDS             1
                  REQUIRED PURSUANT TO THIS SUBSECTION (5)(f) AVAILABLE UPON REQUEST TO               2
                  THE STUDENT'S AUTHORIZED EMERGENCY CONTACT LISTED IN THE STUDENT'S                  3
                  OFFICIAL INSTITUTIONAL RECORD OR LEGAL GUARDIAN IF THE STUDENT HAS NOT              4
                  BEEN LOCATED WITHIN THIRTY DAYS AFTER THE INSTITUTION RECEIVES A                    5
                  MISSING PERSON REPORT.                                                              6
                          (g) (I) CONDUCTING A PRELIMINARY WELLNESS ASSESSMENT PURSUANT               7
                  TO SUBSECTION (5)(d) OF THIS SECTION IS A PERMISSIBLE DISCLOSURE                    8
                  PURSUANT TO THE HEALTH OR SAFETY EMERGENCY EXCEPTION OF THE FEDERAL                 9
                  "FAMILY EDUCATIONAL RIGHTS AND PRIVACY ACT OF 1974", 20 U.S.C. SEC.                10
                  1232g (b)(1)(I), AND DOES NOT CONSTITUTE A VIOLATION OF A STATE STUDENT            11
                  PRIVACY LAW.                                                                       12
                          (II) A DISCLOSURE MADE AS PART OF A PRELIMINARY WELLNESS                   13
                  ASSESSMENT MUST BE LIMITED TO INFORMATION NECESSARY TO LOCATE THE                  14
                  STUDENT AND MUST NOT BE USED FOR ANY OTHER PURPOSE.                                15
                          (h) AS USED IN THIS SUBSECTION (5), UNLESS THE CONTEXT OTHERWISE           16
                  REQUIRES:                                                                          17
                          (I) "ACADEMIC AND SOCIAL INQUIRY" MEANS A QUERY BY AN                      18
                  INSTITUTION OF AVAILABLE FACULTY MEMBERS AND RESIDENTIAL STAFF ABOUT               19
                  THE STUDENT'S MOST RECENTLY KNOWN ATTENDANCE OR SOCIAL INTERACTION                 20
                  SUBJECT TO THE PERMISSIBLE DISCLOSURE PROVISIONS OF SUBSECTION (5)(g) OF           21
                  THIS SECTION.                                                                      22
                          (II) "CIRCUMSTANCES BEYOND THE INSTITUTION'S REASONABLE                    23
                  CONTROL" MEANS AN UNFORESEEABLE SITUATION, OR A SITUATION THE                      24
                  INSTITUTION OF HIGHER EDUCATION IS UNABLE TO ADEQUATELY RESPOND TO,                25
                  INCLUDING, BUT NOT LIMITED TO:                                                     26
                          (A) THE UNAVAILABILITY OF FACULTY OR STAFF OUTSIDE OF REGULAR              27
                  BUSINESS HOURS;                                                                    28
                          (B) THE STUDENT'S RESIDENCE BEING LOCATED OFF CAMPUS OR                    29
                  OUTSIDE THE INSTITUTION'S PHYSICAL JURISDICTION; AND                               30
                          (C) AN INCORRECT, DISCONNECTED, OR UNANSWERED EMERGENCY                    31
                  CONTACT.                                                                           32
                          (III) "DIGITAL CONTACT ATTEMPT" MEANS AN ATTEMPT BY THE                    33
                  INSTITUTION OF HIGHER EDUCATION TO CONTACT THE STUDENT THROUGH ALL                 34
                  INSTITUTION-PROVIDED COMMUNICATIONS AVAILABLE TO THE INSTITUTION,                  35
                  INCLUDING, BUT NOT LIMITED TO, AN INSTITUTIONAL EMAIL, STUDENT PORTAL              36
                  SYSTEM, AND EMERGENCY NOTIFICATION SYSTEM.                                         37
                          (IV) "EMERGENCY CONTACT ATTEMPT" MEANS AN ATTEMPT BY THE                   38
                  INSTITUTION TO REACH THE STUDENT'S EMERGENCY CONTACT PERSON LISTED                 39
                  IN THE STUDENT'S OFFICIAL INSTITUTIONAL RECORD.                                    40
                          (V) "INSTITUTION OF HIGHER EDUCATION" OR "INSTITUTION" MEANS A             41
                  STATE INSTITUTION OF HIGHER EDUCATION, AS DEFINED IN SECTION 23-18-102             42
                  (10)(a); A LOCAL DISTRICT COLLEGE; AN AREA TECHNICAL COLLEGE; THE                  43
                  AURARIA HIGHER EDUCATION CENTER; AN EDUCATION CENTER; A TECHNICAL                  44
                  COLLEGE; A PRIVATE COLLEGE OR UNIVERSITY, AS DEFINED IN SECTION                    45
                  23-2-102; AND A PRIVATE OCCUPATIONAL SCHOOL, AS DEFINED IN SECTION                 46
                   23-2-102.                                                                         47
                          (VI) "REGULAR BUSINESS HOURS" MEANS THE HOURS DURING WHICH                 48
                   THE INSTITUTION OF HIGHER EDUCATION'S ADMINISTRATIVE OFFICES ARE                  49
                   REGULARLY OPEN FOR BUSINESS, AS PUBLISHED IN THE INSTITUTION'S OFFICIAL           50
                   ACADEMIC CALENDAR.                                                                51
                          (VII) "RESIDENTIAL VERIFICATION" MEANS A PHYSICAL CHECK OF THE             52
                   STUDENT'S RESIDENCE IF THE STUDENT RESIDES IN INSTITUTION-CONTROLLED              53
                   HOUSING BY AN AUTHORIZED REPRESENTATIVE OF THE INSTITUTION, AS DEFINED            54
                   BY THE INSTITUTION'S PUBLISHED PRELIMINARY WELLNESS ASSESSMENT POLICY             55
                   REQUIRED PURSUANT TO SUBSECTION (5)(e) OF THIS SECTION.".                         56
