                           "SECTION 1. Legislative declaration. (1) The general assembly            62
                   finds and declares that:                                                         63
                           (a) Every Colorado family deserves a fair, dignified, and understandable 64
                   path to financial assistance when seeking health care. Patients benefit from     65
                   hospitals' discounted care programs and these programs increase access to        66
                   affordable care. Reducing duplication and confusion in navigating the process    67
Senate Journal-101st Day-April 24, 2026                                                  Page 881


    for both patients and health-care providers is essential to ensure the process                   1
    does not create barriers for the very people the law was intended to help.                       2
            (b) Rising insurance premiums and the impacts of H.R. 1 of the 119th                     3
    congress (2025-2026), Pub.L. 119-21, are likely to increase the number of                        4
    uninsured and underinsured Coloradans seeking discounted care. At a time                         5
    when more families are struggling to afford basic health-care services, Colorado                 6
    must ensure that access to financial relief is simple, timely, and centered on the               7
    needs of patients.                                                                               8
            (c) It is the intent of the general assembly to reduce unnecessary                       9
    paperwork, eliminate avoidable burdens, and create a process that respects                      10
    people's time, circumstances, and dignity. Streamlining and clarifying these                    11
    pathways will allow health-care providers to focus more resources on helping                    12
    families instead of on navigating shifting rules or administrative obstacles.                   13
            (d) The general assembly affirms that all patient rights, including the                 14
    right to appeal and to provide information demonstrating eligibility for public                 15
    health-care coverage or discounted care, must remain fully protected; and                       16
            (e) This act strengthens the promise that discounted care in our state                  17
    will be accessible and rooted in compassion.                                                    18
            SECTION 2. In Colorado Revised Statutes, amend 12-30-114 as                             19
    follows:                                                                                        20
            12-30-114. Demonstrated competency - repeal of rules - repeal.                          21
            (1) (a) The regulator for each licensed health-care provider, in                        22
    consultation with the center for research into substance use disorder prevention,               23
    treatment, and recovery support strategies created in section 27-80-118, shall                  24
    promulgate rules that require each licensed health-care provider, as a condition                25
    of renewing, reactivating, or reinstating a license on or after October 1, 2022,                26
    to complete up to four credit hours of training per licensing cycle in order to                 27
    demonstrate competency regarding:                                                               28
            (I) Best practices for opioid prescribing, according to the most recent                 29
    version of the division's guidelines for the safe prescribing and dispensing of                 30
    opioids;                                                                                        31
            (II) The potential harm of inappropriately limiting prescriptions to                    32
    chronic pain patients;                                                                          33
            (III) Best practices for prescribing benzodiazepines;                                   34
            (IV) Recognition of substance use disorders;                                            35
            (V) Referral of patients with substance use disorders for treatment; and                36
            (VI) The use of the electronic prescription drug monitoring program                     37
    created in part 4 of article 280 of this title 12.                                              38
            (b) The rules promulgated by each regulator shall exempt a licensed                     39
    health-care provider who:                                                                       40
            (I) Maintains a national board certification that requires equivalent                   41
    substance use prevention training; or                                                           42
            (II) Attests to the regulator that the health-care provider does not                    43
    prescribe opioids.                                                                              44
            (2) For the purposes of this section, "licensed health-care provider"                   45

    12:                                                                                             47
            (a) A physician;                                                                        48

                          "SECTION 1. Short title. The short title of this act is the "Promoting         17
                 Responsible End-of-Life Management of Electric Vehicle Batteries Act".                  18
                          SECTION 2. In Colorado Revised Statutes, 25-17-1002, amend (2);                19
                 and add (1.5) as follows:                                                               20
                          25-17-1002. Legislative declaration.                                           21
                          (1.5) THE GENERAL ASSEMBLY FURTHER FINDS THAT:                                 22
                          (a) ELECTRIC VEHICLES ARE CRUCIAL TOOLS FOR REDUCING                           23
                 GREENHOUSE GAS EMISSIONS, WHICH THE STATE IS STRIVING TO ELIMINATE BY                   24
                 2050. ELECTRIC VEHICLES ARE ALSO VITAL TO REDUCING LOCAL AIR POLLUTION                  25
                 IN AREAS OF THE STATE, SUCH AS THE DENVER METRO AND NORTH FRONT                         26
                 RANGE AREAS, THAT THE FEDERAL ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY HAS                       27
                 DESIGNATED AS BEING IN NONATTAINMENT WITH A NATIONAL AMBIENT AIR                        28
                 QUALITY STANDARD. TO ACHIEVE EMISSION REDUCTIONS NEEDED TO MEET                         29
                 STATE-MANDATED CLIMATE GOALS AND FEDERALLY REQUIRED OZONE LEVELS,                       30
                 MANY MORE ELECTRIC VEHICLES WILL NEED TO BE DEPLOYED IN COLORADO.                       31
                          (b) AS ELECTRIC VEHICLE SALES IN THE STATE CONTINUE TO GROW,                   32
                 SUBSTANTIALLY MORE ELECTRIC VEHICLES WILL BE RETIRED IN THE COMING                      33
                 YEARS, AND THEIR BATTERIES, KNOWN AS PROPULSION BATTERIES, WILL NEED                    34
                 RESPONSIBLE END-OF-LIFE MANAGEMENT;                                                     35
                          (c) PROPULSION BATTERIES OFTEN RETAIN VALUE EVEN AFTER THEY                    36
                 CEASE TO POWER THE ORIGINAL VEHICLES INTO WHICH THEY WERE PLACED AND                    37
                 CAN BE REUSED, REMANUFACTURED, REPURPOSED, OR RECYCLED. EXTENDING                       38
                 THE USEFUL LIFESPAN OF PROPULSION BATTERIES IMPROVES THE                                39
                 SUSTAINABILITY PROFILE OF THE ELECTRIC VEHICLE INDUSTRY AND CREATES                     40
                 LOCAL ECONOMIC OPPORTUNITIES.                                                           41
                          (d) MULTIPLE ANALYSES HAVE ESTABLISHED THAT EXPENSIVE AND                      42
                 HAZARDOUS RISKS RESULT FROM THE IMPROPER HANDLING, STORAGE, AND                         43
                 DISPOSAL OF PROPULSION BATTERIES; AND                                                   44
                          (e) UNWANTED PROPULSION BATTERIES THAT ARE STORED IMPROPERLY                   45
                 INSTEAD OF BEING SORTED FOR REUSE, REMANUFACTURING, REPURPOSING, OR                     46
                 ULTIMATE RECYCLING AND RECOVERY OF VALUABLE MATERIALS COULD                             47
                 POTENTIALLY REDUCE THE ENVIRONMENTAL BENEFITS OF A ROBUST CIRCULAR                      48
                 ECONOMY FOR PROPULSION BATTERIES WHILE ALSO INCREASING THE RISK OF                      49
                 BATTERY FIRES. A ROBUST EXTENDED PROVIDER RESPONSIBILITY POLICY IS                      50
                 NEEDED TO ENABLE A PROPULSION BATTERY CIRCULAR ECONOMY.                                 51
                          (2) The general assembly therefore declares that it is in the public           52
                 interest of Colorado to:                                                                53
                          (a) Require producers of batteries AND PROVIDERS OF PROPULSION                 54
                 BATTERIES to finance and implement a coordinated, state-approved system that            55
                 increases access to the safe disposal AND RESPONSIBLE END-OF-LIFE                       56
                 MANAGEMENT of batteries in Colorado;                                                    57
                          (b) REDUCE THE INHERENT RISK OF FIRE THAT CAN OCCUR WHEN                       58
                 PROPULSION BATTERIES ARE IMPROPERLY DISPOSED OF; AND                                    59
                          (c) ENCOURAGE THE REUSE, REMANUFACTURING, AND REPURPOSING OF                   60
                 PROPULSION BATTERIES AND THE ULTIMATE RECYCLING AND RECOVERY OF THE                     61
                 VALUABLE MATERIALS IN A PROPULSION BATTERY THAT CAN BE PUT BACK INTO                    62
                 THE SUPPLY CHAIN.                                                                       63

    (e) ANY PLEDGE OF THE FUND IS VALID AND BINDING FROM THE TIME THE                     23
    PLEDGE IS MADE. THE PLEDGED FUND IS IMMEDIATELY SUBJECT TO THE LIEN OF                24
    THE PLEDGE WITHOUT ANY PHYSICAL DELIVERY OR FURTHER ACT, AND THE LIEN                 25
    OF THE PLEDGE IS VALID AND BINDING AGAINST ALL PARTIES HAVING CLAIMS OF               26
    ANY KIND IN TORT, CONTRACT, OR OTHERWISE AGAINST THE PLEDGING PARTY                   27
    REGARDLESS OF WHETHER THE CLAIMING PARTY HAS NOTICE OF THE LIEN. THE                  28
    INSTRUMENT BY WHICH THE PLEDGE IS CREATED NEED NOT BE RECORDED OR                     29
    FILED.                                                                                30
    (f) NEITHER THE MEMBERS OF THE BOARD, NOR EMPLOYEES OF THE                            31
    ENTERPRISE, NOR ANY PERSON EXECUTING THE BONDS IS LIABLE PERSONALLY                   32
    ON THE BONDS OR SUBJECT TO ANY PERSONAL LIABILITY BY REASON OF THE                    33
    ISSUANCE OF THE BONDS.                                                                34
    (g) THE ENTERPRISE MAY PURCHASE ITS BONDS OUT OF ANY AVAILABLE MONEY                  35
    AND MAY HOLD, PLEDGE, CANCEL, OR RESELL SUCH BONDS SUBJECT TO AND IN                  36
    ACCORDANCE WITH AGREEMENTS WITH THE BOND HOLDERS.                                     37
    (2) THE ENTERPRISE MAY INVEST OR DEPOSIT ANY PROCEEDS AND ANY                         38
    INTEREST FROM THE SALE OF BONDS IN THE MANNER PROVIDED BY PART 6 OF                   39
    ARTICLE 75 OF TITLE 24. IN ADDITION, AN ISSUING ENTERPRISE MAY DIRECT A               40
    CORPORATE TRUSTEE THAT HOLDS THE BOND PROCEEDS AND ANY INTEREST TO                    41
    INVEST OR DEPOSIT THE PROCEEDS AND INTEREST IN INVESTMENTS OR DEPOSITS                42
    OTHER THAN THOSE SPECIFIED BY SAID PART 6 IF THE BOARD DETERMINES, BY                 43
    RESOLUTION, THAT THE INVESTMENT OR DEPOSIT MEETS THE STANDARD                         44
    ESTABLISHED IN SECTION 15-1-304, THE INCOME IS AT LEAST COMPARABLE TO                 45
    INCOME AVAILABLE ON INVESTMENTS OR DEPOSITS SPECIFIED BY SAID PART 6,                 46
    AND THE INVESTMENT WILL ASSIST THE ENTERPRISE IN FUNDING PROGRAMS                     47
    SPECIFIED IN THIS PART 12.                                                            48
    (3) ALL BANKS, TRUST COMPANIES, SAVINGS AND LOAN ASSOCIATIONS,                        49
    INSURANCE COMPANIES, EXECUTORS, ADMINISTRATORS, GUARDIANS, TRUSTEES,                  50
    AND OTHER FIDUCIARIES MAY LEGALLY INVEST ANY MONEY WITHIN THEIR                       51
    CONTROL IN ANY BONDS ISSUED UNDER THIS PART 12. PUBLIC ENTITIES, AS                   52
    DEFINED IN SECTION 24-75-601 (1), MAY INVEST PUBLIC MONEY IN SUCH BONDS               53
    ONLY IF THE BONDS SATISFY THE INVESTMENT REQUIREMENTS ESTABLISHED IN                  54
    PART 6 OF ARTICLE 75 OF TITLE 24.                                                     55
    (4) THE INCOME OR OTHER REVENUES OF THE ENTERPRISE, BONDS ISSUED BY                   56
    THE ENTERPRISE, AND THE TRANSFER OF AND THE INCOME FROM ANY BONDS                     57
    ISSUED BY THE ENTERPRISE ARE EXEMPT FROM ALL TAXATION AND                             58
    ASSESSMENTS IN THE STATE. IN THE RESOLUTION OR INDENTURE AUTHORIZING                  59
    THE BONDS, THE ENTERPRISE MAY WAIVE THE EXEMPTION FROM FEDERAL                        60
    INCOME TAXATION FOR INTEREST ON THE BONDS. BONDS ISSUED BY THE                        61
    ENTERPRISE ARE EXEMPT FROM THE PROVISIONS OF ARTICLE 51 OF TITLE 11.".                62
                                                                                          63
    Renumber succeeding sections accordingly.                                             64

          "SECTION 53. In Colorado Revised Statutes, repeal and reenact,                   18
    with amendments, 1-9-101 as follows:                                                   19
          1-9-101. Challenge of incorrect registration. (1) (a) ANY                        20
    REGISTERED ELECTOR MAY PROTEST THE REGISTRATION OF ANY PERSON WHOSE                    21
    NAME APPEARS IN A COUNTY REGISTRATION RECORD FOR THE COUNTY IN WHICH                   22
    THE CHALLENGING ELECTOR RESIDES. A PROTEST MAY CHALLENGE A PERSON'S                    23
    REGISTRATION AS INCORRECT BECAUSE THE PERSON IS:                                       24
           (I) NOT A CITIZEN OF THE UNITED STATES;                                         25
           (II) NOT A LEAST FIFTEEN YEARS OLD;                                             26
           (III) DECEASED; OR                                                              27
           (IV) NO LONGER A RESIDENT OF THE STATE, BUT HAS NOT YET BEEN                    28
    MARKED "INACTIVE" IN THE VOTER REGISTRATION RECORD.                                    29
           (b) A PROTEST MUST BE SUBMITTED FOR EACH PERSON WHOSE                           30
    REGISTRATION IS BEING CHALLENGED. THE PROTEST MUST BE MADE IN WRITING                  31
    ON A FORM PRESCRIBED BY THE SECRETARY OF STATE AND MUST INCLUDE:                       32
           (I) THE NAME OF THE PERSON WHOSE REGISTRATION IS CHALLENGED;                    33
           (II) THE BASIS FOR THE CHALLENGE, INCLUDING SUPPORTING FACTS;                   34
           (III) ALL DOCUMENTARY EVIDENCE SUPPORTING THE FACTUAL BASIS                     35
    FOR THE CHALLENGE; AND                                                                 36
           (IV) THE SIGNATURE AND ADDRESS OF THE CHALLENGER.                               37
           (c) A PROTEST MUST BE FILED WITH THE COUNTY CLERK AND RECORDER                  38
    OF THE COUNTY WHERE THE CHALLENGED REGISTRATION RECORD RESIDES NO                      39
    LATER THAN ONE HUNDRED TWENTY DAYS BEFORE ANY ELECTION CONDUCTED                       40
    BY THAT COUNTY CLERK AND RECORDER. A PROTEST FEE OF FIFTY DOLLARS                      41
    MUST BE PAID TO THE COUNTY CLERK AND RECORDER RESPONSIBLE FOR                          42
    ADJUDICATING THE CHALLENGE AT THE TIME THAT A PROTEST IS SUBMITTED. A                  43
    FEE PAYMENT IS REQUIRED FOR EACH WRITTEN PROTEST. IF A PROTEST IS                      44
    SUCCESSFUL, THE PROTEST FEE MUST BE REFUNDED TO THE CHALLENGER.                        45
           (d) UPON RECEIPT OF A PROTEST, A COUNTY CLERK AND RECORDER                      46
    SHALL REVIEW THE PROTEST TO DETERMINE IF IT SUFFICIENTLY ALLEGES A BASIS               47
    FOR A CHALLENGE IN ACCORDANCE WITH SUBSECTION (1)(a) OF THIS SECTION.                  48
    IF A PROTEST DOES NOT ALLEGE A SUFFICIENT BASIS FOR A CHALLENGE                        49
    PURSUANT TO THIS SECTION, THE COUNTY CLERK AND RECORDER SHALL DISMISS                  50
    THE CHALLENGE AND NOTIFY THE CHALLENGER OF THE DISMISSAL. IF A PROTEST                 51
    SUFFICIENTLY ALLEGES A BASIS FOR A CHALLENGE PURSUANT TO THIS SECTION,                 52
    THE COUNTY CLERK AND RECORDER SHALL NOTIFY AND MAIL A COPY OF THE                      53
    CHALLENGE TO THE PERSON WHOSE REGISTRATION IS BEING CHALLENGED. THE                    54
    COUNTY CLERK AND RECORDER SHALL NOTIFY THE PERSON WHOSE                                55
    REGISTRATION IS BEING CHALLENGED AND THE CHALLENGER OF THE DATE,                       56
    TIME, AND LOCATION SET FOR THE CHALLENGE HEARING REQUIRED BY                           57
    SUBSECTION (1)(e) OF THIS SECTION.                                                     58
           (e) IF A COUNTY CLERK AND RECORDER DETERMINES THAT A PROTEST                    59
    SUFFICIENTLY ALLEGES A BASIS FOR A CHALLENGE PURSUANT TO THIS SECTION,                 60
    THEN THE COUNTY CLERK AND RECORDER MUST SET A HEARING DATE THAT IS                     61
    NO LATER THAN THIRTY DAYS FROM THE DATE THE PROTEST WAS FILED AND                      62
    MUST PROVIDE NOTICE IN ACCORDANCE WITH SUBSECTION (1)(d) OF THIS                       63
    SECTION. THE CHALLENGER WHO SUBMITTED THE PROTEST MUST APPEAR AT                       64
    THE HEARING AND SHALL BEAR THE BURDEN OF PROVING THE ALLEGATIONS                       65
    MADE IN THE PROTEST ARE TRUE. THE PERSON WHOSE REGISTRATION IS BEING                   66
    CHALLENGED MUST HAVE THE OPPORTUNITY TO APPEAR AT THE HEARING, BUT                     67
Page 1028   Senate Journal-108th Day-May 1, 2026


                MAY NOT BE PENALIZED OR SUBJECT TO A NEGATIVE PRESUMPTION OR                      1
                INFERENCE IF THEY DO NOT APPEAR. THE COUNTY CLERK AND RECORDER SHALL              2
                CONDUCT THE HEARING AND MAY RECEIVE EVIDENCE AND HEAR TESTIMONY.                  3
                NO LATER THAN FIVE DAYS AFTER THE DATE OF THE HEARING, BUT IN NO EVENT            4
                LATER THAN NINETY DAYS BEFORE AN ELECTION CONDUCTED BY THE COUNTY                 5
                CLERK AND RECORDER, THE COUNTY CLERK AND RECORDER MUST RENDER A                   6
                DECISION IN ACCORDANCE WITH SUBSECTION (1)(f) OF THIS SECTION AND                 7
                NOTIFY BOTH PARTIES OF THE DECISION.                                              8
                        (f) IN RENDERING A DECISION AFTER THE HEARING ON A PROTEST, A             9
                COUNTY CLERK AND RECORDER MUST PROCEED AS FOLLOWS:                               10
                        (I) IF THEY FIND SUFFICIENT EVIDENCE TO SUPPORT THE ALLEGATIONS          11
                IN THE PROTEST, AND THE BASIS OF THE CHALLENGE IS THAT THE PERSON IS             12
                DECEASED, LESS THAN FIFTEEN YEARS OLD, OR NOT A CITIZEN OF THE UNITED            13
                STATES, THE COUNTY CLERK AND RECORDER SHALL CANCEL THE PERSON'S                  14
                VOTER REGISTRATION RECORD IN THE STATEWIDE VOTER REGISTRATION                    15
                SYSTEM;                                                                          16
                        (II) IF THEY FIND SUFFICIENT EVIDENCE TO SUPPORT THE ALLEGATIONS         17
                IN THE PROTEST, AND THE BASIS FOR THE CHALLENGE IS THAT THE PERSON IS            18
                NOT A RESIDENT OF THE STATE, THE COUNTY CLERK AND RECORDER SHALL                 19
                MARK THE PERSON'S VOTER REGISTRATION RECORD "INACTIVE", SEND A                   20
                CONFIRMATION CARD, AND OTHERWISE FOLLOW THE REQUIREMENTS OF SECTION              21
                1-2-302.5; OR                                                                    22
                        (III) IF THEY DO NOT FIND SUFFICIENT EVIDENCE TO SUPPORT THE             23
                ALLEGATIONS IN THE PROTEST, THE COUNTY CLERK AND RECORDER SHALL DENY             24
                THE CHALLENGE.                                                                   25
                        (2) ALL APPEALS FROM A DECISION OF THE COUNTY CLERK AND                  26
                RECORDER MUST BE TO THE DISTRICT COURT AND FILED WITHIN THREE DAYS               27
                FROM THE DATE THE DECISION IS ISSUED. AN APPELLANT MUST FILE IN THE              28
                DISTRICT COURT A VERIFIED PETITION SETTING FORTH THE FACTS PRESENTED AT          29
                THE HEARING, IF ANY, THE DECISION OF THE COUNTY CLERK AND RECORDER,              30
                AND THE BASIS FOR THE APPEAL. WITHIN TWENTY-FOUR HOURS, THE CLERK OF             31
                THE DISTRICT COURT MUST MAIL TO THE OTHER PARTY A NOTICE OF THE                  32
                APPEAL, INCLUDING THE TIME OF ANY HEARING. A HEARING MUST BE HELD NO             33
                LESS THAN THREE DAYS NOR MORE THAN FIVE DAYS AFTER THE DATE THE                  34
                VERIFIED PETITION IS FILED.                                                      35
                        (3) (a) A DISTRICT COURT MUST HEAR TESTIMONY AND OTHER                   36
                EVIDENCE AND INVESTIGATE SUMMARILY ANY APPEAL FILED PURSUANT TO                  37
                SUBSECTION (2) OF THIS SECTION. ONLY COMPETENT LEGAL EVIDENCE MAY BE             38
                RECEIVED AT THE HEARING OR CONSIDERED BY THE COURT. NO PRESUMPTION               39
                MAY BE MADE AGAINST A PERSON WHOSE REGISTRATION IS CHALLENGED                    40
                MERELY BECAUSE OF THEIR FAILURE TO ATTEND THE HEARING. THE COURT HAS             41
                THE POWER TO SUBPOENA ANY PERSON AS A WITNESS AND TO MAKE ANY                    42
                NECESSARY INVESTIGATION TO ASCERTAIN THE TRUTH OF ANY CHARGES MADE               43
                IN THE PETITION, IF THE METHOD OF INVESTIGATION DOES NOT CAUSE                   44
                UNNECESSARY DELAY OR INTERFERE WITH THE FINAL DISPOSITION OF THE                 45
                PROTEST WITHIN THE TIME PROVIDED IN THIS SECTION. A HEARING ON ANY               46
                PETITION IS SUMMARY AND FINAL AND IS NOT SUBJECT TO DELAY.                       47
                        (b) AT THE CLOSE OF THE HEARING, THE COURT MUST ANNOUNCE IF THE          48
                PROTEST HAS BEEN SUSTAINED. IF THE PROTEST IS SUSTAINED, THE COURT               49
                SHALL ORDER THE APPROPRIATE REMEDY IN ACCORDANCE WITH SUBSECTION                 50
                (1)(f) OF THIS SECTION. THE COURT SHALL DIRECT THE CLERK OF THE COURT TO         51
                CERTIFY THE NAME OF THE PERSON WHOSE REGISTRATION IS CHALLENGED AND              52
                THE REMEDY TO THE COUNTY CLERK AND RECORDER. UPON RECEIPT OF THE                 53
                NAME AND REMEDY, THE COUNTY CLERK AND RECORDER SHALL TAKE THE                    54
                ACTION REQUIRED BY THE COURT. THE DECISION OF THE COURT IS FINAL AND             55
                NOT SUBJECT TO REVIEW BY ANY OTHER COURT; EXCEPT THAT THE SUPREME                56
                COURT, IN ITS DISCRETION, MAY REVIEW ANY SUCH PROCEEDINGS IN A SUMMARY           57
                WAY.".                                                                           58

                                                                                                        6
           Catherine Kunz                                                                               7
                                                                                                        8
           For her work on behalf of the Colorado Channel and the People of Colorado. The General 9
           Assembly recognizes the service of Catherine Kunz as she concludes her work with The 10
           Colorado Channel after nine legislative sessions. Throughout her tenure, Catherine played 11
           a vital role in preserving public access to this body's proceedings and ensuring that the   12
           legislature's work was accurately recorded and reliably transmitted to the people of        13
           Colorado. She also contributed meaningfully to The Colorado Channel's continuity by         14
           mentoring new staff and upholding a culture of excellence. Beyond her professional          15
           contributions, Catherine brought a spirit of generosity that enriched the Capitol           16
           community. The General Assembly extends its gratitude for her service and wishes her        17
           well in the years ahead.                                                                    18

    TO EVALUATE AND MAKE RECOMMENDATIONS CONCERNING FUNDING STATE                         13
    AND LOCAL SURFACE TRANSPORTATION MAINTENANCE, REPAIR, CAPACITY, AND                   14
    SAFETY.                                                                               15
           (3) THE DEPARTMENT SHALL CONTRACT WITH A NEUTRAL FACILITATOR                   16
    TO ORGANIZE AND MANAGE THE WORKING GROUP'S MEETINGS, GUIDE THE                        17
    WORKING GROUP'S DELIBERATIONS, AND DRAFT THE REPORTS REQUIRED                         18
    PURSUANT TO SUBSECTIONS (7)(a) AND (7)(b) OF THIS SECTION.                            19
           (4) (a) THE WORKING GROUP CONSISTS OF THE FOLLOWING MEMBERS:                   20
           (I) THE EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR OR THE EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR'S DESIGNEE;               21
           (II) ONE MEMBER APPOINTED BY THE GOVERNOR WITH EXPERTISE IN                    22
    PUBLIC FINANCE;                                                                       23
           (III) ONE MEMBER APPOINTED BY THE GOVERNOR TO REPRESENT                        24
    ENVIRONMENTAL CONSERVATION OR ENVIRONMENTAL JUSTICE GROUPS;                           25
           (IV) ONE MEMBER APPOINTED BY THE SPEAKER OF THE HOUSE OF                       26
    REPRESENTATIVES TO REPRESENT COUNTIES ACROSS THE STATE;                               27
           (V) ONE MEMBER APPOINTED BY THE SPEAKER OF THE HOUSE OF                        28
    REPRESENTATIVES TO REPRESENT LICENSED PROFESSIONAL ENGINEERS;                         29
           (VI) ONE MEMBER APPOINTED BY THE MINORITY LEADER OF THE HOUSE                  30
    OF REPRESENTATIVES TO REPRESENT AN ASSOCIATION OF MOTOR CARRIERS;                     31
           (VII) ONE MEMBER APPOINTED BY THE PRESIDENT OF THE SENATE TO                   32
    REPRESENT MUNICIPALITIES ACROSS THE STATE;                                            33
           (VIII) ONE MEMBER APPOINTED BY THE PRESIDENT OF THE SENATE TO                  34
    REPRESENT ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT ORGANIZATIONS; AND                                     35
           (IX) ONE MEMBER APPOINTED BY THE MINORITY LEADER OF THE                        36
    SENATE TO REPRESENT CONSTRUCTION CONTRACTOR PROFESSIONALS.                            37
           (b) THE APPLICABLE APPOINTING AUTHORITIES SHALL MAKE ALL OF THE                38
    APPOINTMENTS DESCRIBED IN SUBSECTION (4)(a) OF THIS SECTION NO LATER                  39
    JUNE 19, 2026.                                                                        40
           (c) MEMBERS OF THE WORKING GROUP SERVE AT THE PLEASURE OF THE                  41
    APPLICABLE APPOINTING AUTHORITY. IF A VACANCY OCCURS, THE APPROPRIATE                 42
    APPOINTING AUTHORITY SHALL APPOINT A REPLACEMENT MEMBER WHO MEETS                     43
    THE REQUIREMENTS SET FORTH IN SUBSECTION (4)(a) OF THIS SECTION FOR THE               44
    VACANT POSITION NOT LATER THAN ONE WEEK FROM THE DATE THE VACANCY                     45
    EXISTS. IF THE APPROPRIATE APPOINTING AUTHORITY FAILS TO APPOINT A                    46
    REPLACEMENT MEMBER AS REQUIRED BY THIS SUBSECTION (4)(c), THE                         47
    GOVERNOR SHALL APPOINT A REPLACEMENT MEMBER WHO MEETS THE                             48
    REQUIREMENTS SET FORTH IN SUBSECTION (4)(a) OF THIS SECTION.                          49
           (d) MEMBERS OF THE WORKING GROUP SERVE WITHOUT COMPENSATION                    50
    AND WITHOUT REIMBURSEMENT FOR EXPENSES.                                               51
           (e) MEMBERS OF THE WORKING GROUP MAY PARTICIPATE REMOTELY IN                   52
    WORKING GROUP MEETINGS.                                                               53
           (5) (a) THE FACILITATOR SHALL CONVENE THE FIRST MEETING OF THE                 54
    WORKING GROUP DURING THE WEEK OF JUNE 29, 2026. THE WORKING GROUP                     55
    SHALL ADOPT BYLAWS AT THE FIRST WORKING GROUP MEETING.                                56
           (b) THE WORKING GROUP SHALL MEET AT LEAST ONCE EVERY TWO                       57
    WEEKS BEGINNING THE WEEK OF JUNE 29, 2026, THROUGH THE WEEK OF                        58
    NOVEMBER 2, 2026. THE WORKING GROUP MAY MEET MORE OFTEN AT THE                        59
    DISCRETION OF THE FACILITATOR. A MAJORITY OF THE MEMBERS OF THE                       60
    WORKING GROUP MAY VOTE TO EXTEND THE WORK OF THE COMMISSION PAST                      61
    THE WEEK OF NOVEMBER 2, 2026, OR TO TERMINATE THE WORKING GROUP'S                     62
    WORK AT ANY TIME.                                                                     63
           (c) THE WORKING GROUP MAY MEET WITH SUBJECT MATTER EXPERTS                     64
    AS NEEDED, SUCH AS EXPERTS ON THE STATE BUDGET, PUBLIC FINANCING, AND                 65
    TRANSPORTATION CONSTRUCTION.                                                          66
           (6) THE WORKING GROUP'S PURPOSE IS TO IDENTIFY APPROACHES TO                   67
Page 1210   Senate Journal-118th Day-May 11, 2026


                AUGMENT STATE AND LOCAL FUNDING FOR SURFACE TRANSPORTATION                          1
                MAINTENANCE, REPAIR, CAPACITY, AND SAFETY BY INCREASING REVENUE,                    2
                WHILE FOCUSING ON INCREASING REVENUE THAT IS PROTECTED FOR SUCH                     3
                PURPOSES, IS SUSTAINABLE, AND DOES NOT NECESSITATE CUTS TO CORE STATE               4
                AND LOCAL SERVICES.                                                                 5
                       (7) (a) NO LATER THAN SEPTEMBER 7, 2026, THE WORKING GROUP                   6
                SHALL SUBMIT A PRELIMINARY STATUS REPORT TO THE TRANSPORTATION,                     7
                HOUSING, AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE OF                             8
                REPRESENTATIVES, THE TRANSPORTATION AND ENERGY COMMITTEE OF THE                     9
                SENATE, THE TRANSPORTATION COMMISSION CREATED IN SECTION 43-1-106,                 10
                AND THE GOVERNOR. THE REPORT MUST INCLUDE:                                         11
                       (I) A SUMMARY OF THE WORKING GROUP'S DISCUSSIONS AND FINDINGS;              12
                AND                                                                                13
                       (II) THE POTENTIAL STATE BUDGETARY IMPACTS, AS DISCUSSED BY THE             14
                WORKING GROUP, OF POTENTIAL APPROACHES TO AUGMENT STATE AND LOCAL                  15
                FUNDING FOR SURFACE TRANSPORTATION MAINTENANCE, REPAIR, CAPACITY,                  16
                AND SAFETY NEEDS.                                                                  17
                       (b) NO LATER THAN NOVEMBER 13, 2026, THE WORKING GROUP SHALL                18
                SUBMIT A REPORT TO THE TRANSPORTATION, HOUSING, AND LOCAL                          19
                GOVERNMENT COMMITTEE OF THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, THE                          20
                TRANSPORTATION AND ENERGY COMMITTEE OF THE SENATE, THE                             21
                TRANSPORTATION COMMISSION CREATED IN SECTION 43-1-106, AND THE                     22
                GOVERNOR. THE REPORT MUST INCLUDE THE WORKING GROUP'S FINDINGS AND                 23
                RECOMMENDATIONS TO THE GENERAL ASSEMBLY CONCERNING MATTERS                         24
                EVALUATED BY THE WORKING GROUP.                                                    25
                       (8) (a) THE DEPARTMENT SHALL BE AVAILABLE TO ASSIST THE WORKING             26
                GROUP IN CARRYING OUT THE WORKING GROUP'S DUTIES. THE DEPARTMENT                   27
                MAY ADOPT INTERNAL PROCEDURES TO ENSURE THAT THE WORKING GROUP'S                   28
                WORK IS CONDUCTED IN AN ORDERLY, TIMELY, AND GOAL-ORIENTED MANNER.                 29
                       (b) NOTWITHSTANDING ANY LAW TO THE CONTRARY, THE DEPARTMENT                 30
                MAY EXPEND MONEY FROM THE STATE HIGHWAY FUND, CREATED IN SECTION                   31
                43-1-219, FOR THE WORKING GROUP'S PURPOSES INCLUDING FOR HIRING                    32
                PROFESSIONAL FACILITATION SERVICES, ASSISTING THE WORKING GROUP                    33
                PURSUANT TO SUBSECTION (8)(a) OF THIS SECTION, AND OTHER NECESSARY                 34
                SERVICES.                                                                          35
                       (9) THIS SECTION IS REPEALED, EFFECTIVE JULY 1, 2027.".                     36

    customer-facing programs - legislative declaration - definitions.                    1
           (6) (a) THE GENERAL ASSEMBLY FINDS AND DECLARES THAT:                         2
           (I) SINCE 2007, COLORADO HAS ENACTED SEVERAL STATUTES THAT                    3
    DIRECT COMMISSION-REGULATED INVESTOR-OWNED UTILITIES TO IMPLEMENT                    4
    CUSTOMER-FACING PROGRAMS AIMED AT REDUCING ENERGY BILLS, REDUCING                    5
    ENERGY CONSUMPTION, OR SUPPORTING THE TRANSITION TO LOWER- OR                        6
    ZERO-CARBON-EMITTING TECHNOLOGIES;                                                   7
           (II) SUCH CUSTOMER-FACING PROGRAMS INCLUDE DEMAND-SIDE                        8
    MANAGEMENT, BENEFICIAL ELECTRIFICATION, CLEAN HEAT PLANS, AND                        9
    TRANSPORTATION ELECTRIFICATION;                                                     10
           (III) FOR MANY OF THESE PROGRAMS, UTILITIES MAY LACK A NATURAL               11
    INCENTIVE TO TAKE CERTAIN ACTIONS OR IMPLEMENT THESE PROGRAMS                       12
    EFFECTIVELY. ADDITIONALLY, DUE TO STAFFING OR ECONOMIES OF SCALE,                   13
    SMALLER UTILITIES MAY LACK THE ABILITY TO OPERATE SUCH PROGRAMS AT A                14
    REASONABLE COST TO RATEPAYERS.                                                      15
            (IV)     CERTAIN RATEPAYER AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS ARE                       16
    IMPLEMENTED BY A THIRD PARTY THAT WAS NOT SELECTED THROUGH A                        17
    COMPETITIVE PROCESS, AND THERE IS LIMITED OVERSIGHT OF THE THIRD                    18
    PARTY'S USE OF RATEPAYER DOLLARS;                                                   19
            (V) ESTABLISHED STATE ENTERPRISES, SUCH AS THE BUILDING                     20
    DECARBONIZATION ENTERPRISE CREATED IN SECTION 24-38.5-125, MAY                      21
    PROVIDE AN ALTERNATIVE OPTION FOR ADMINISTERING COMPETITIVE                         22
    SOLICITATIONS FOR THIRD-PARTY PROGRAM ADMINISTRATION; AND                           23
            (VI) THEREFORE, THE COMMISSION SHOULD BE AUTHORIZED TO                      24
    REQUIRE COMMISSION-REGULATED INVESTOR-OWNED UTILITIES TO ENGAGE ONE                 25
    OR MORE THIRD PARTIES TO ADMINISTER SPECIFIC CUSTOMER-FACING                        26
    PROGRAMS IF THE COMMISSION DEEMS THE USE OF ONE OR MORE THIRD PARTIES               27
    PRUDENT AND IN THE BEST INTEREST OF RATEPAYERS. IN ADDITION, THE                    28
    COMMISSION SHOULD BE AUTHORIZED TO REQUIRE THE USE OF A COMPETITIVE                 29
    BIDDING PROCESS TO PROCURE THE SERVICES OF A THIRD-PARTY                            30
    ADMINISTRATOR.                                                                      31
            (b) IN AN ADJUDICATORY PROCEEDING, THE COMMISSION MAY REQUIRE               32
    A COMMISSION-REGULATED INVESTOR-OWNED UTILITY TO ENGAGE ONE OR                      33
    MORE THIRD PARTIES TO ADMINISTER SPECIFIC CUSTOMER-FACING PROGRAMS                  34
    IF THE COMMISSION DEEMS THE USE OF ONE OR MORE THIRD PARTIES PRUDENT                35
    AND IN THE BEST INTEREST OF RATEPAYERS. THE COMMISSION MAY REQUIRE A                36
    COMPETITIVE BIDDING PROCESS TO PROCURE THE SERVICES OF A THIRD-PARTY                37
    ADMINISTRATOR.                                                                      38
            (c) AS USED IN THIS SUBSECTION (6), "CUSTOMER-FACING PROGRAM"               39
    MEANS A PROGRAM AIMED AT REDUCING ENERGY BILLS, REDUCING ENERGY                     40
    CONSUMPTION, OR SUPPORTING THE TRANSITION TO LOWER- OR                              41
    ZERO-CARBON-EMITTING TECHNOLOGIES.                                                  42
            (7) (a) A COMMISSION-REGULATED INVESTOR-OWNED UTILITY MAY                   43
    ENTER INTO A THIRD-PARTY AGREEMENT TO FACILITATE CUSTOMER-FACING                    44
    PROGRAMS, SUBJECT TO COMMISSION APPROVAL. THE COMMISSION MAY DIRECT                 45
    A COMMISSION-REGULATED INVESTOR-OWNED UTILITY TO PROPOSE TO THE                     46
    COMMISSION THE USE OF THIRD - PARTY ADMINISTRATION FOR                              47
    CUSTOMER-FACING PROGRAMS.                                                           48
            (b) IN A COMMISSION-REGULATED INVESTOR-OWNED UTILITY'S                      49
    PROPOSAL TO UTILIZE THIRD-PARTY ADMINISTRATION OF A CUSTOMER-FACING                 50
    PROGRAM, THE UTILITY SHALL EXPLAIN TO THE COMMISSION HOW THE UTILITY                51
    CONSIDERED THE FOLLOWING IN RELATION TO THE CUSTOMER-FACING                         52
    PROGRAM:                                                                            53
            (I) THE POTENTIAL FOR PROGRAM SUCCESS BASED ON AN ASSESSMENT                54
    OF SIMILAR ADMINISTRATION STRUCTURES THAT OTHER UTILITIES USE FOR                   55
    SIMILAR CUSTOMER-FACING PROGRAMS;                                                   56
            (II) THE ADMINISTRATIVE COST RATIO OF ADMINISTERING REBATES                 57
    VERSUS THE INCENTIVES PAID OUT AS PART OF THE PROGRAM;                              58
            (III) THE TIME REQUIRED TO FULFILL CUSTOMER REBATE REQUESTS;                59
    AND                                                                                 60
            (IV) PRIOR PROGRAM PERFORMANCE UNDER A UTILITY-LED MODEL.                   61
            (c) IN AN APPLICATION TO THE COMMISSION TO ENTER INTO A                     62
    THIRD-PARTY AGREEMENT TO FACILITATE CUSTOMER-FACING PROGRAMS, THE                   63
    UTILITY MAY NOT:                                                                    64
            (I) FORCE A LAYOFF OF, OR UNILATERALLY CHANGE THE TERMS OF                  65
    EMPLOYMENT FOR, THE UTILITY EMPLOYEES WHO, IN WHOLE OR IN PART,                     66
    PERFORM THE ADMINISTRATIVE OR SERVICE FUNCTIONS FOR THE SPECIFIC                    67

                                                                                                                49
              The Senate of                                                                                     50
              The Colorado Legislature                                                                          51
              Convened in the Second Regular Session of the Seventy-Fifth General Assembly                      52
              Hereby acknowledges service to the State of Colorado by the Southern Ute Indian Tribe             53
                                                                                                                54
              In December 2024, the 40-year-old Enterprise pipeline within the exterior boundaries of the       55
              Southern Ute Reservation failed, releasing an estimated 200,000 gallons of gasoline into the      56
              surrounding environment. Following the spill, CDPHE failed to address the significant health      57
              concerns and threats to the environment within the Reservation, while Enterprise dramatically     58
              understated the scale of the disaster and engaged in no earnest remediation.                      59
              Consequently, the Tribe launched its own independent investigation. Tribal consultants identified 60
              contamination across more than 110 acres of the drinking water aquifer, with the gasoline plume 61
              migrating approximately 10 feet per day. Reservation residents have lost access to drinking water 62
              wells and, in some cases, their homes, while others remain at risk as contamination continues to  63
              spread. CDPHE and the Attorney General must fully investigate and address this disaster. The      64
              dedication of the Southern Ute Indian Tribe on this issue is deeply appreciated and will not be   65
              forgotten.                                                                                        66

             "SECTION 23. In Colorado Revised Statutes, add part 17 to article 4               20
    of title 43 as follows:                                                                    21
                                     PART 17                                                   22
                               ROAD ENTERPRISE                                                 23
             43-4-1701. Legislative declaration.                                               24
             (1) THE GENERAL ASSEMBLY FINDS AND DECLARES THAT:                                 25
             (a) THE CONTINUED PROSPERITY OF THE STATE AND ITS CITIZENS                        26
    REQUIRES A SAFE, WELL-MAINTAINED, INTEGRATED, MULTIMODAL, AND                              27
    SUSTAINABLE SURFACE TRANSPORTATION SYSTEM THAT IS ACCESSIBLE IN ALL                        28
    PARTS OF THE STATE AND THAT ALLOWS EFFICIENT MOVEMENT OF PEOPLE,                           29
    GOODS, AND INFORMATION;                                                                    30
           (b) THE STATE HIGHWAY SYSTEM IS A FUNDAMENTAL ELEMENT OF THE                        31
    SURFACE TRANSPORTATION SYSTEM AND THE CONDITION OF THE ROADWAYS                            32
    COMPRISING THE STATE HIGHWAY SYSTEM ARE ESSENTIAL TO THE EFFICIENT                         33
    MOVEMENT OF PEOPLE, GOODS, AND INFORMATION;                                                34
           (c) THE CONDITION OF THE STATE HIGHWAY SYSTEM, IN PARTICULAR                        35
    THE CONDITION OF THE ROADWAY SURFACE, HAS DETERIORATED OVER TIME AS                        36
    A RESULT OF THE AGING OF THE SYSTEM AND INCREASED DEMANDS UPON IT,                         37
    INCLUDING GROWING POPULATION AND VEHICLE MILES TRAVELED;                                   38
           (d) IN PARTICULAR OVERSIZE AND OVERWEIGHT VEHICLES AND LONGER                       39
    VEHICLE COMBINATIONS CAUSE A DISPROPORTIONATE AMOUNT OF WEAR AND                           40
    TEAR ON THE STATE'S HIGHWAY SYSTEM;                                                        41
           (e) THERE IS AN URGENT PRESENT NEED TO IMPROVE THE CONDITION OF                     42
    THE STATE HIGHWAY SYSTEM THROUGH INCREASED INVESTMENT IN PREVENTIVE                        43
    MAINTENANCE, REPAIR, REHABILITATION, AND RECONSTRUCTION OF THE                             44
    ROADWAY SURFACE; AND                                                                       45
           (f) DUE TO THE LIMITED AVAILABILITY OF STATE AND FEDERAL                            46
    FUNDING AND THE NEED TO COMPLETE PREVENTIVE MAINTENANCE, REPAIR,                           47
    REHABILITATION, AND RECONSTRUCTION PROJECTS TO IMPROVE THE CONDITION                       48
    OF THE ROADWAY SURFACE OF THE STATE HIGHWAY SYSTEM AND TO SUPPORT                          49
    THE ONGOING MAINTENANCE OF THE ROADWAY SURFACE, IT IS NECESSARY TO                         50
    CREATE A ROAD ENTERPRISE AND TO AUTHORIZE THE ENTERPRISE TO:                               51
           (I) COMPLETE PREVENTIVE MAINTENANCE, REPAIR, REHABILITATION,                        52
    AND RECONSTRUCTION PROJECTS TO IMPROVE THE CONDITION OF THE ROADWAY                        53
    SURFACE OF THE STATE HIGHWAY SYSTEM AND TO SUPPORT THE ONGOING                             54
    MAINTENANCE OF THE ROADWAY SURFACE; AND                                                    55
           (II) IMPOSE PERMIT FEES FOR OVERSIZE AND OVERWEIGHT VEHICLES                        56
    AND LONGER VEHICLE COMBINATIONS AT RATES REASONABLY CALCULATED TO                          57
    DEFRAY THE COSTS OF MAINTAINING THE ROADWAY SURFACES OF THE STATE                          58
    HIGHWAY SYSTEM, RECEIVE AND EXPEND REVENUE GENERATED BY THE PERMIT                         59
    FEES AND OTHER MONEY, ISSUE REVENUE BONDS AND OTHER OBLIGATIONS, AND                       60
    EXERCISE OTHER POWERS NECESSARY AND APPROPRIATE TO CARRY OUT ITS                           61
    PURPOSES.                                                                                  62
           (2) THE GENERAL ASSEMBLY FURTHER FINDS AND DECLARES THAT:                           63
           (a) THE ROAD ENTERPRISE PROVIDES BUSINESSES SERVICES WHEN, IN                       64
    EXCHANGE FOR THE PAYMENT OF PERMIT FEES FOR OVERSIZE AND OVERWEIGHT                        65
    VEHICLES AND LONGER VEHICLE COMBINATIONS, IT COMPLETES PREVENTIVE                          66
    MAINTENANCE, REPAIR, REHABILITATION, AND RECONSTRUCTION PROJECTS TO                        67
Page 1270   Senate Journal-120th Day-May 13, 2026


                IMPROVE THE CONDITION OF THE ROADWAY SURFACE OF THE STATE HIGHWAY          1
                SYSTEM AND SUPPORTS THE ONGOING MAINTENANCE OF THE ROADWAY                 2
                SURFACE;                                                                   3
                        (b) BY COMPLETING ROADWAY SURFACE PROJECTS AS SERVICES AS          4
                AUTHORIZED BY THIS SECTION, THE ROAD ENTERPRISE PROVIDES A BENEFIT TO      5
                FEE PAYERS BY IMPROVING THE CONDITION OF THE ROADWAY SURFACE OF THE        6
                STATE HIGHWAY SYSTEM THAT OFFSETS THE WEAR AND TEAR CAUSED BY THOSE        7
                FEE PAYERS AND, THEREFORE, OPERATES AS A BUSINESS IN ACCORDANCE WITH       8
                THE DETERMINATION OF THE COLORADO SUPREME COURT IN COLORADO UNION          9
                OF TAXPAYERS FOUNDATION V. CITY OF ASPEN, 2018 CO 36;                     10
                        (c) CONSISTENT WITH THE DETERMINATION OF THE COLORADO             11
                SUPREME COURT IN NICHOLL V. E-470 PUBLIC HIGHWAY AUTHORITY, 896 P.2d      12
                859 (COLO. 1995), THE POWER TO IMPOSE TAXES IS INCONSISTENT WITH          13
                ENTERPRISE STATUS UNDER SECTION 20 OF ARTICLE X OF THE STATE              14
                CONSTITUTION, AND, THEREFORE, IT IS THE CONCLUSION OF THE GENERAL         15
                ASSEMBLY THAT THE REVENUE COLLECTED BY THE ROAD ENTERPRISE IS             16
                GENERATED BY FEES, NOT TAXES, BECAUSE THE PERMIT FEES FOR OVERSIZE AND    17
                OVERWEIGHT VEHICLES AND LONGER VEHICLE COMBINATIONS IMPOSED BY THE        18
                ENTERPRISE ARE:                                                           19
                        (I) IMPOSED FOR THE SPECIFIC PURPOSE OF ALLOWING THE ENTERPRISE   20
                TO DEFRAY THE COSTS OF PROVIDING THE SERVICES SPECIFIED IN SECTION        21
                43-4-1703 (2); AND                                                        22
                        (II) COLLECTED AT RATES THAT ARE REASONABLY CALCULATED BASED      23
                ON THE COSTS OF THE SERVICES PROVIDED BY THE ENTERPRISE;                  24
                        (d) SO LONG AS THE ENTERPRISE QUALIFIES AS AN ENTERPRISE FOR      25
                PURPOSES OF SECTION 20 OF ARTICLE X OF THE STATE CONSTITUTION, THE        26
                REVENUE FROM PERMIT FEES FOR OVERSIZE AND OVERWEIGHT VEHICLES AND         27
                LONGER VEHICLE COMBINATIONS IS NOT STATE FISCAL YEAR SPENDING, AS         28
                DEFINED IN SECTION 24-77-102 (17), OR STATE REVENUES, AS DEFINED IN       29
                SECTION 24-77-103.6 (6)(c), AND DOES NOT COUNT AGAINST EITHER THE STATE   30
                FISCAL YEAR SPENDING LIMIT IMPOSED BY SECTION 20 OF ARTICLE X OF THE      31
                STATE CONSTITUTION OR THE EXCESS STATE REVENUES CAP, AS DEFINED IN        32
                SECTION 24-77-103.6 (6)(b)(I)(G); AND                                     33
                        (e) NO OTHER ENTERPRISE CREATED SIMULTANEOUSLY OR WITHIN THE      34
                PRECEDING FIVE YEARS SERVES PRIMARILY THE SAME PURPOSE AS THE ROAD        35
                ENTERPRISE, AND THE ROAD ENTERPRISE WILL GENERATE REVENUE FROM            36
                PERMIT FEES OF LESS THAN ONE HUNDRED MILLION DOLLARS TOTAL IN ITS FIRST   37
                FIVE FISCAL YEARS. ACCORDINGLY, THE CREATION OF THE ROAD ENTERPRISE       38
                DOES NOT REQUIRE VOTER APPROVAL PURSUANT TO SECTION 24-77-108.            39
                       43-4-1702. Definitions.                                            40
                       AS USED IN THIS PART 17, UNLESS THE CONTEXT OTHERWISE REQUIRES:    41
                       (1) "ENTERPRISE" MEANS THE ROAD ENTERPRISE CREATED IN SECTION      42
                43-4-1703.                                                                43
                       (2) "FEES" MEANS THE PERMIT FEES FOR OVERSIZE AND OVERWEIGHT       44
                VEHICLES AND LONGER VEHICLE COMBINATIONS IMPOSED BY THE ENTERPRISE        45
                AND COLLECTED PURSUANT TO SECTIONS 42-4-505 AND 42-4-510.                 46
                      (3) "FUND" MEANS THE ROAD ENTERPRISE CASH FUND CREATED IN           47
                SECTION 43-4-1704 (1).                                                    48
                      43-4-1703. Road enterprise - creation - powers and duties.          49
                      (1) (a)    THE ROAD ENTERPRISE IS AND OPERATES AS A                 50
                GOVERNMENT-OWNED BUSINESS WITHIN THE DEPARTMENT IN ORDER TO               51
                EXECUTE ITS BUSINESS PURPOSE AS SPECIFIED IN SUBSECTION (2) OF THIS       52
                SECTION BY EXERCISING THE POWERS AND PERFORMING THE DUTIES AND            53
                FUNCTIONS SET FORTH IN THIS SECTION. THE TRANSPORTATION COMMISSION        54
                CREATED IN SECTION 43-1-106 (1) SHALL SERVE AS THE ENTERPRISE BOARD AND   55
                SHALL, WITH THE CONSENT OF THE EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR, APPOINT AN             56
                ENTERPRISE DIRECTOR WHO POSSESSES SUCH QUALIFICATIONS AS THE              57
                COMMISSION AND THE STATE PERSONNEL BOARD MAY ESTABLISH. THE               58
                ENTERPRISE DIRECTOR SHALL OVERSEE THE DISCHARGE OF ALL                    59
                RESPONSIBILITIES OF THE ENTERPRISE AND SHALL SERVE AT THE PLEASURE OF     60
                THE ENTERPRISE BOARD.                                                     61
                       (b) THE ENTERPRISE IS A TYPE 1 ENTITY, AS DEFINED IN SECTION       62
                24-1-105, AND EXERCISES ITS POWERS AND PERFORMS ITS DUTIES AND            63
                FUNCTIONS UNDER THE DEPARTMENT. THE GOVERNING BOARD OF THE                64
                ENTERPRISE IS MADE UP OF THE TRANSPORTATION COMMISSION CREATED IN         65
                SECTION 43-1-106 (1).                                                     66
                       (2) (a) THE BUSINESS PURPOSE OF THE ENTERPRISE IS TO COMPLETE      67
Senate Journal-120th Day-May 13, 2026                                          Page 1271


    PREVENTIVE MAINTENANCE, REPAIR, REHABILITATION, AND RECONSTRUCTION                      1
    PROJECTS TO IMPROVE THE CONDITION OF THE ROADWAY SURFACE OF THE                         2
    STATE HIGHWAY SYSTEM AND TO SUPPORT THE ONGOING MAINTENANCE OF THE                      3
    ROADWAY SURFACE.                                                                        4
           (b) TO ALLOW THE ENTERPRISE TO ACCOMPLISH THIS PURPOSE AND                       5
    FULLY EXERCISE ITS POWERS AND DUTIES THROUGH THE ENTERPRISE BOARD,                      6
    THE ENTERPRISE MAY:                                                                     7
           (I) IMPOSE FEES AS AUTHORIZED BY SECTION 43-4-1705 (1);                          8
           (II) ISSUE REVENUE BONDS PAYABLE FROM THE REVENUES AND OTHER                     9
    AVAILABLE MONEY OF THE ENTERPRISE PLEDGED FOR THEIR PAYMENT;                           10
           (III) SEEK, ACCEPT, AND EXPEND MONEY FROM FEDERAL SOURCES; AND                  11
           (VI) SEEK, ACCEPT, AND EXPEND GIFTS, GRANTS, AND DONATIONS.                     12
           (3) THE ENTERPRISE CONSTITUTES AN ENTERPRISE FOR PURPOSES OF                    13
    SECTION 20 OF ARTICLE X OF THE STATE CONSTITUTION SO LONG AS IT RETAINS                14
    THE AUTHORITY TO ISSUE REVENUE BONDS AND RECEIVES LESS THAN TEN                        15
    PERCENT OF ITS TOTAL ANNUAL REVENUE IN GRANTS FROM ALL COLORADO                        16
    STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS COMBINED. SO LONG AS IT CONSTITUTES AN                     17
    ENTERPRISE PURSUANT TO THIS SUBSECTION (3), THE ENTERPRISE IS NOT                      18
    SUBJECT TO SECTION 20 OF ARTICLE X OF THE STATE CONSTITUTION.                          19
           (4) IN ADDITION TO ANY OTHER POWERS AND DUTIES SPECIFIED IN THIS                20
    SECTION, THE ENTERPRISE HAS THE FOLLOWING GENERAL POWERS AND DUTIES:                   21
           (a) TO PROVIDE SERVICES AS SET FORTH IN SUBSECTION (2) OF THIS                  22
    SECTION; AND                                                                           23
           (b) TO HAVE AND EXERCISE ALL RIGHTS AND POWERS NECESSARY OR                     24
    INCIDENTAL TO OR IMPLIED FROM THE SPECIFIC POWERS AND DUTIES GRANTED                   25
    BY THIS SECTION.                                                                       26
            43-4-1704. Road enterprise cash fund.                                          27
            (1) THE ROAD ENTERPRISE CASH FUND IS CREATED IN THE STATE                      28
    TREASURY. THE FUND CONSISTS OF FEES THAT THE STATE TREASURER CREDITS                   29
    TO THE FUND PURSUANT TO SECTIONS 42-4-505 (1)(d) AND 42-4-510 (11)(c);                 30
    GIFTS, GRANTS, AND DONATIONS; AND ANY OTHER MONEY THAT THE GENERAL                     31
    ASSEMBLY MAY APPROPRIATE OR TRANSFER TO THE FUND.                                      32
            (2) THE STATE TREASURER SHALL CREDIT ALL INTEREST AND INCOME                   33
    DERIVED FROM THE DEPOSIT AND INVESTMENT OF MONEY IN THE FUND TO THE                    34
    FUND.                                                                                  35
           (3) MONEY IN THE FUND IS CONTINUOUSLY APPROPRIATED TO THE                       36
    ENTERPRISE FOR THE DIRECT AND INDIRECT COSTS OF SERVING ITS BUSINESS                   37
    PURPOSE AND IN PERFORMING ITS POWERS AND DUTIES AS THE PURPOSE,                        38
    POWERS, AND DUTIES ARE SET FORTH IN SECTION 43-4-1703 (2).                             39
           (4) THE DEPARTMENT MAY TRANSFER MONEY FROM ANY LEGALLY                          40
    AVAILABLE SOURCE TO THE ENTERPRISE FOR THE PURPOSE OF DEFRAYING                        41
    EXPENSES INCURRED BY THE ENTERPRISE BEFORE IT RECEIVES FEE REVENUE OR                  42
    REVENUE BOND PROCEEDS. THE ENTERPRISE MAY ACCEPT AND EXPEND ANY                        43
    MONEY SO TRANSFERRED, AND, NOTWITHSTANDING ANY STATE FISCAL RULE OR                    44
    GENERALLY ACCEPTED ACCOUNTING PRINCIPLE THAT COULD OTHERWISE BE                        45
    INTERPRETED TO REQUIRE A CONTRARY CONCLUSION, SUCH A TRANSFER IS A                     46
    LOAN FROM THE DEPARTMENT TO THE ENTERPRISE THAT IS REQUIRED TO BE                      47
    REPAID AND IS NOT A GRANT FOR PURPOSES OF SECTION 20 (2)(d) OF ARTICLE X               48
    OF THE STATE CONSTITUTION OR AS DEFINED IN SECTION 24-77-102 (7). ALL                  49
    MONEY TRANSFERRED AS A LOAN TO THE ENTERPRISE MUST BE CREDITED TO                      50
    THE FUND. AS THE ENTERPRISE RECEIVES SUFFICIENT REVENUE IN EXCESS OF                   51
    EXPENSES, THE ENTERPRISE SHALL REIMBURSE THE DEPARTMENT FOR THE                        52
    PRINCIPAL AMOUNT OF ANY LOAN MADE BY THE DEPARTMENT PLUS INTEREST                      53
    AT A RATE SET BY THE DEPARTMENT.                                                       54
           43-4-1705. Road enterprise fees.                                                55
           (1) IN FURTHERANCE OF ITS BUSINESS PURPOSE, BEGINNING JANUARY                   56
    1, 2027, THE ENTERPRISE SHALL IMPOSE FEES FOR OVERSIZE AND OVERWEIGHT                  57
    VEHICLES AND LONGER VEHICLE COMBINATIONS.                                              58
           (2) FOR THE PURPOSE OF MINIMIZING COMPLIANCE COSTS FOR FEE                      59
    PAYERS AND ADMINISTRATIVE COSTS, THE DEPARTMENT, AS DESCRIBED IN                       60
    SECTIONS 42-4-505 (1)(d) AND 42-4-510 (11)(c), SHALL PERFORM THE                       61
    COLLECTION, ADMINISTRATION, AND ENFORCEMENT OF THE FEES IMPOSED BY                     62
    THE ENTERPRISE PURSUANT TO SUBSECTION (1) OF THIS SECTION.                             63
           (3) AS REQUIRED BY SECTIONS 42-4-505 (1)(d) AND 42-4-510 (11)(c),               64
    THE DEPARTMENT SHALL TRANSMIT ANY FEE REVENUE IT COLLECTS TO THE                       65
    STATE TREASURER, WHO SHALL CREDIT THE REVENUE, MINUS THE COSTS TO THE                  66
    DEPARTMENT FOR COLLECTING THE FEES, TO THE FUND.".                                     67

            200 East Colfax Avenue                                                                          1
            Denver, CO 80203                                                                                2
                                                                                                            3
            Dear Honorable Members of the Colorado State Senate,                                            4
                                                                                                            5
            Today, I signed Senate Bill 26-149 (SB26-l49), "Pathways for Individuals with Mental            6
            Health Disorder," at 11:30 am.                                                                  7
                                                                                                            8
            When someone is a serious danger to themselves or others, they should be connected to           9
            services and secure, safe placement. SB26-l49 contains critical policies to protect public 10
            safety across the state of Colorado by closing dangerous gaps in our competency system. 11
            Before today, when an individual was found incompetent to proceed to trial and unlikely 12
            to be restored in the near future, courts were required to dismiss the criminal cases of       13
            these individuals, no matter how serious the charges, at times releasing individuals with      14
            violent history and tendencies from custody without necessary services or security             15
            considerations. The status quo fails to protect the public and meet the complex needs of       16
            these individuals and can even undermine the important work we are doing together to           17
            make Colorado one of the ten safest states.                                                    18
                                                                                                           19
            This bipartisan legislation dramatically improves our ability to connect defendants to         20
            services when they have been found incompetent and unlikely to be restored. It empowers 21
            the state to find safe and appropriate placements for individuals whose criminal cases         22
            have been dismissed, whether they need disability services or mental health services. For 23
            individuals who have committed very serious crimes and present a substantial risk of harm 24
            to themselves or others, this legislation ensures the individual receives secure placement 25
            that accounts for the individual's medical needs and community safety.                         26
                                                                                                           27
            As state agencies implement SB26-149, they will break new ground - both literally and          28
            metaphorically. The Department of Human Services will expand placements at the                 29
            Colorado Mental Health Hospital in Pueblo, contract for additional capacity with private 30
            providers across the state, and begin work on a new outpatient clinic, all of which will       31
            deliver much-needed services to patients in the competency system. In collaboration with 32
            their colleagues at the Department of Health Care Policy and Financing and the                 33
            Behavioral Health Administration, they will also assess patients, identify the most            34
            appropriate placement for their needs, and help to ensure that civil commitments or            35
            protective placement orders are lifted only when appropriate. This work requires               36
            extraordinary state investment and extensive work across executive agencies and our            37
            judicial partners.                                                                             38
                                                                                                           39
            SB26-l49 is an imperative first step in addressing issues that arise when individuals are      40
            incompetent and unrestorable. As with any policy and investment that is so substantial,        41
            there are unknowns that lie ahead. The state is now funded to serve an estimated 46            42
            individuals under a civil commitment or enhanced protective placement; the actual              43
            volume of patients may be higher or lower, and the duration of these stays is similarly        44
            impossible to know for sure. These issues contribute to overall uncertainty around the         45
            annual cost of this measure, including what services may be reimbursable under Medicaid. 46
            It is our intent to bring emergency requests for additional funding to the Joint Budget        47
            Committee should Departments reach the end of their funded capacity to fulfill the terms 48
            of this law.                                                                                   49
                                                                                                           50
            The bill calls on several partners across the executive branch and other government            51
            agencies - including Bridges of Colorado, the Office of the Public Guardian, and county 52
            attorneys - to work together in serving these individuals. While this structure provides       53
            flexibility for essential collaboration, it will also require the establishment of clear roles 54
            and responsibilities. To conduct this work, I expect executive branch agencies to utilize      55
            established coordination and placement functions, and serve their respective patient           56
            populations as funded, authorized by law, and appropriate. The affected agencies will          57
            establish interagency guidance that outlines the processes for conducting this work, and       58
            make continued recommendations for increased efficiencies or more appropriate                  59
            reassignments to the Governor's Office as necessary. I also expect agencies to operate         60
            within the bounds of state and federal law and regulation, and abide by the terms of           61
            federal and state court precedent wherever applicable.                                         62
                                                                                                           63
            SB26-149 also makes adjustments to the civil mental health system in Colorado, distinct 64
            from the new pathways for individuals who are incompetent and unrestorable. I applaud 65
            the sponsors' intent in these provisions: to give courts and clinicians the right tools to     66
            support individuals with chronic behavioral health needs who may not seek help                 67
            voluntarily. These changes must be implemented carefully in order to balance clinical          68
            considerations and promote effective and appropriate treatment access - all while              69
            balancing the capacity of the system.                                                          70
                                                                                                           71
            My administration looks forward to working closely with stakeholder partners and the           72
 Senate Journal-Addendum                                                         Page 1283


 General Assembly as we implement this legislation and identify any necessary                 1
 adjustments to ensure smooth operation.                                                      2
                                                                                              3
 At 176 pages, SB26-149 is the second longest measure of the 2026 session behind only         4
 the long bill. The bill itself is a testament to the breadth of intensive negotiation and    5
 collaboration across myriad stakeholders, including prosecutors, public defenders, health    6
 care providers, and disability and mental health advocates. It passed unanimously through 7
 House and Senate Judiciary Committees, and both chamber floors thanks to the work of         8
 its strong bipartisan sponsors, Senator Judy Amabile, Minority Leader Cleave Simpson,        9
 Speaker Julie McCluskie, and Minority Leader Jarvis Caldwell. I express my deep             10
 gratitude for those who contributed to this measure: we should all be very proud of this    11
 joint effort to make Colorado safer.                                                        12
                                                                                             13
    Sincerely,                                                                               14
    (signed)                                                                                 15
    Jared Polis                                                                              16
    Governor                                                                                 17
    State of Colorado                                                                        18

            Dear Honorable Members of the Colorado State Senate,                                          29
                                                                                                          30
            Today, I signed into law Senate Bill 26-125 (SB26-125) "Disability Rights Protections in 31
            Public Schools."                                                                              32
                                                                                                          33
            In 1973, Congress passed The Rehabilitation Act ("The Act"), with Section 504 of that         34
            law prohibiting organizations who receive federal funding from discriminating on the          35
            basis of disability, among other things. The Act, and Section 504, remain in effect today, 36
            protecting the rights of Coloradans with disabilities. SB 26-125 codifies into state law the 37
            protections afforded by The Act and its implementing regulations as they pertain to           38
            students with disabilities and sets forth a potential enforcement pathway through the         39
            Colorado Department of Education (CDE).                                                       40
                                                                                                          41
            I applaud the sponsors' commitment to ensure families receiving section 504 services have 42
            a more easily navigable pathway to bring f01ward complaints at the state level through        43
            CDE, in addition to their existing pathways through their local school district, at the       44
            Colorado Civil Rights Division (CCRD), the federal Office of Civil Rights within the          45
            U.S. Department of Education, or state or federal courts. This is even more critical as the 46
            Federal Government has not prioritized enforcement of these important rights. Without a 47
            pathway for enforcement, too many families that choose not to bring their complaints          48
            through existing pathways will wait months or even years to have their complaints heard 49
            and their services remedied. As any parent understands, time is of the essence when it        50
            comes to ensuring their children receive the services they need to succeed in school.         51
                                                                                                          52
            Unfortunately, SB26-125 charges the Colorado Department of Education (CDE) with               53
            enforcement of the law, but only if CDE receives adequate funding in the next two years 54
            from gifts, grants, donations, and "other agreements for resources," including through        55
            contracts with third parties or other state agencies. CDE estimates they will need over       56
            $650,000 to operationalize the enforcement program and more than $500,000 annually for 57
            on-going staffing to enforce this law.                                                        58
                                                                                                          59
            To-date, such funding has not been identified, and I believe strongly that this language      60
            sets a dangerous precedent for how to fund core government services, especially               61
            something as critical as civil rights enforcement, which should never be on-again,            62
            off-again based on receipt of adequate charitable donations. Setting up CDE to receive        63
            funds from organizations they may have to enforce also creates a potential conflict of        64
            interest. While grants, gifts, and donations can be appropriate and have been used to fund 65
            studies, grant programs, task forces, and other one time efforts, this mechanism should not 66
            be used to fund core regulatory functions.                                                    67
                                                                                                          68
            Despite this problematic funding mechanism, I support the sponsors' desire to reiterate       69
            federal disability protections for all students in Colorado and to reaffirm school districts' 70
            obligations to uphold those protections. While current 504 regulations charge school          71
            districts with ensuring students are free from disability discrimination, SB26-l25 provides 72
Senate Journal-Addendum                                                              Page 1287


clear requirements for training, resource dedication, and a step-by-step grievance process      1
to assist school districts in effectively implementing those disability protections. It is also 2
why I will be working with the Colorado Department of Education to submit a FY26-27             3
supplemental budget request and an FY27-28 budget request to adequately fund this law.          4
Prior to receiving funds from the General Assembly, I encourage CDE not to rely on the          5
untenable and unsustainable funding mechanism of gifts, grants, and donations for core          6
civil rights protection efforts like this for core civil rights protection efforts like this.   7
                                                                                                8
Protections for students with disabilities are far too important to rely on gifts, grants, and  9
donations, and must be adequately funded expeditiously.                                        10
                                                                                               11
   Sincerely,                                                                                  12
   (signed)                                                                                    13
   Jared Polis                                                                                 14
   Governor                                                                                    15
