Dear Honorable Members of the Colorado State Senate,                                           29
                                                                                               30
Today, I vetoed Senate Bill 26-147 (SB26-147) "Lobbyist Regulation" at 12:55 pm.               31
                                                                                               32
Signing this bill would be a very mean thing to do to future Governors, as it infringes on 33
their ability to independently gather information and evaluate legislation as it moves         34
through the General Assembly, and to make ultimate determinations on bills once they           35
reach the desk of the Governor- as is the Governor's Constitutional responsibility.            36
                                                                                               37
This bill requires individuals advocating on behalf of the Offices of the Governor and         38
Lieutenant Governor to register annually and file a monthly disclosure statement with the 39
Secretary of State that includes their position on legislation, requires individuals           40
responsible for advocating on behalf of the Judicial Department and their independent          41
agencies to register with the Secretary of State and disclose their positions on bills,        42
requires legislative liaisons representing Executive Branch agencies to disclose an            43
agency's position on bills, and makes other changes related to lobbyist registration. I have 44
long-championed government transparency, including by opposing efforts to weaken the 45
Colorado Open Records Act and by authoring Amendment 41. I am concerned, however, 46
that SB26-l 47 will not lead to more transparency, and instead will erode the separation of 47
powers among the branches of State government as well as impinge on future Governors' 48
independent decision making. I am also troubled that this would make Colorado the only 49
state in the nation so far as we can tell with such requirements placed on the Executive       50
Branch.                                                                                        51
                                                                                               52
Existing law already has certain lobbying disclosure requirements for legislative liaisons 53
representing state agencies and institutions of higher education; the changes in SB26-147 54
would go a step too far. By requiring the disclosure of positions (support, oppose, amend, 55
or monitor) by the Governor and Lieutenant Governor on the legislation that is being           56
lobbied and updating positions within 72 hours of any change, the bill puts the Executive 57
Branch in the same category as professional lobbyists.                                         58
                                                                                               59
The Governor must review, understand, and develop an opinion on every bill that passes 60
the General Assembly and preserve the authority to deliberate over bills until she or he       61
takes final action on legislation. That process is no different than a legislator who          62
considers a bill, talks to stakeholders, and ultimately casts a vote on a bill in the way that 63
they see fit at the appropriate time in the legislative process. That decision is wholly       64
independent, and based on the factors that the individual determines to be relevant.           65
Requiring a Governor to take formal positions prior to final action would impede his or        66
her independent decision making, and make it more challenging for Governor's staff to do 67
what they are often asked to do, which is provide counsel on legislation in the service of 68
winning the Governor's ultimate support.                                                       69
                                                                                               70
While the bill imposes new requirements on two branches of government, it does not             71
propose a requirement that legislators similarly disclose their positions on bills before      72
Page 1288   Senate Journal-Addendum


            their votes. This is an unequal and burdensome infringement that erodes separation of            1
            powers by elevating one branch of government over others, under the guise of                     2
            transparency.                                                                                    3
                                                                                                             4
            To be clear, my administration would not directly face SB26-147's new requirements. I            5
            am only concerned about future Governors. Any Governor has the right to formulate an             6
            opinion and evolve their position on a bill until the moment they take final action on it,       7
            similar to a legislator's right to change their vote up until it is cast. Further, the Governor  8
            must take action on hundreds of bills a year - this year alone, 449 bills (out of 626            9
            introduced) reached my desk and require my consideration. Functionally, no Governor is 10
            in a position to express formal positions on every single bill prior to passage and final       11
            analysis, and yet, this bill would essentially require that very thing.                         12
                                                                                                            13
            I will also just note in closing that my staff has repeatedly told me stories of many           14
            legislators specifically requesting that my office not express a position on various            15
            legislative bills while those bills were pending and were wrapped up in larger                  16
            negotiations, something that would be impossible should this current bill become law.           17
                                                                                                            18
            If the legislature is serious about adding this burden for the next Executive, they should      19
            ensure that sufficient resources are appropriated for the significant extra work required,      20
            and also consider placing a similar requirement on the legislative branch.                      21
                                                                                                            22
            For these reasons, SB26-147 is disapproved and vetoed.                                          23
                                                                                                            24
               Sincerely,                                                                                   25
               (signed)                                                                                     26
               Jared Polis                                                                                  27
               Governor                                                                                     28
               State of Colorado                                                                            29

            Dear Honorable Members of the Colorado State Senate,                                          10
                                                                                                          11
            Today, I vetoed Senate Bill 26-146 (SB 26-146), "Restrict Single-Use Food Serviceware 12
            Distribution," at 3:00 pm.                                                                    13
                                                                                                          14
            This bill prohibits a retail food establishment or third-party food delivery service from     15
            providing single-use food serviceware (including items like utensils, napkins, straws, and 16
            single use condiments) to a customer unless the customer requests single-use food             17
            serviceware or confirms that the customer wants single-use food serviceware after offered. 18
                                                                                                          19
            My administration has been committed to creating a sustainable, affordable and livable        20
            Colorado. We have taken many steps over the last few years to strengthen our recycling        21
            and waste reduction systems and build circular economies, including reducing the use of 22
            single-use plastic bags and styrofoam containers. In partnership with the General             23
            Assembly, we also created the Producer Responsibility Program for paper and packaging, 24
            which will provide free recycling to every resident of our state, saving local governments 25
            money, creating new jobs and providing recycling education and outreach. I appreciate the 26
            sponsors intent to build on these policies to continue to promote waste reduction in our      27
            state.                                                                                        28
                                                                                                          29
            While this bill aims to continue the work our state has done on reducing waste, the state     30
            should not play a role in mandating whether single-use serviceware is provided to             31
            consumers. As the bill itself recognizes by placing the enforcement mechanism at the local 32
            level, local governments should determine whether to implement these policies. Some           33
            local governments in Colorado have decided to pass a similar policy such as Denver and 34
            Breckenridge. I appreciate these efforts, but think statewide policy of this kind is not a    35
            good fit.                                                                                     36
                                                                                                          37
            Ensuring consumer opt-in requires technology that is seamless for restaurants and             38
            consumers. And while several national third party delivery services are already complying, 39
            this does not mean that these services are available throughout Colorado. For instance,       40
            smaller restaurants may lack the technology or receive takeout orders by phone. If a          41
            consumer forgets to check a box or a restaurant forgets to ask a consumer, this may           42
            inconvenience a consumer or cause unnecessary frustration with the restaurant. For            43
            Coloradans who are eating their food on the go, perhaps at a park or another outdoor          44
            space, this could present a significant challenge. Finally, there are always new              45
            technologies looking to enter the delivery space. Burdensome regulations can make it          46
            harder for new entrants to compete in the market.                                             47
                                                                                                          48
            The state should continue to provide local governments and businesses with education          49
            and resources to encourage waste reduction. For example, the "Colorado Circular               50
            Communities Enterprise" or "C3 enterprise" is a statewide program that provides financial 51
            and technical assistance to local governments, businesses, nonprofits, schools, tribes and 52
            higher education institutions to help achieve their waste diversion goals and transition to a 53
            circular economy.                                                                             54
                                                                                                          55
            We want to ensure that Colorado is the best place to live and start a business. The           56
            restaurant and hospitality industry is an integral part of Colorado. Coloradans go to         57
            restaurants to enjoy delicious food, celebrate big events and milestones, and experience      58
            the rich cultures all over our state. We want to break down barriers and give restaurants     59
            the flexibility they need to continue to grow and thrive. Unfortunately, this bill moves us 60
            in the wrong direction.                                                                       61
                                                                                                          62
            For these reasons, SB 26-146 is disapproved and vetoed.                                       63
                                                                                                          64
               Sincerely,                                                                                 65
               (signed)                                                                                   66
               Jared Polis                                                                                67
               Governor                                                                                   68

                                                                                            59
Dear Honorable Members of the Colorado State Senate,                                        60
                                                                                            61
Today, I signed into law Senate Bill 26-003 (SB26-003), "End-of-Life Management of          62
Electric Vehicle Batteries." This bill establishes a framework to ensure responsible end of 63
life management of propulsion batteries - those primarily used to supply power to electric, 64
plug-in hybrid electric or hybrid vehicles - by prohibiting landfilling and prioritizing    65
reuse, repurposing and recycling.                                                           66
                                                                                            67
Colorado is a national leader in electric vehicle (EV) adoption, reaching nearly a third of 68
vehicles sold at the end of last year. EV s are an important tool in improving air quality  69
and saving Coloradans money. Like most vehicles on the road, the current fleet of EV s      70
will remain on the road for years to come. This law aims to ensure that when these          71
vehicles reach the end of their life, the propulsion batteries inside are safely and        72
Page 1292   Senate Journal-Addendum


            responsibly managed. At the same time, it is imperative that we not harm EV adoption or         1
            affordability in Colorado.                                                                      2
                                                                                                            3
            Our state is proud to promote the development of circular economies, which not only             4
            reduce waste but create jobs, incentivize innovative products and solutions, and support a 5
            sustainable future. I support the sponsors' intent to prioritize reuse and recycling of end of 6
            life propulsion batteries that still retain high economic value. They can be repurposed into 7
            new batteries, stationary storage to support and backup the power grid, and other               8
            solutions.                                                                                      9
                                                                                                           10
            This bill fills a gap in the market by ensuring there is an entity responsible (propulsion     11
            battery providers and remanufacturers) for the collection and management of unwanted           12
            propulsion batteries (no longer wanted by the owner) from secondary handlers. These            13
            batteries are most likely to be mismanaged and improperly disposed of if there is not a low 14
            cost or low friction option for secondary handlers to transfer these batteries to an entity    15
            that will ensure proper end-of-life management. It is imperative that all commercial           16
            entities, including secondary handlers, managing propulsion battery waste follow existing 17
            local, state and federal law to ensure safe management, treatment, storage, and disposal of 18
            propulsion batteries. As is current practice, I expect the Colorado Department of Public       19
            Health and Environment (CDPHE) to investigate any credible complaint related to a              20
            violation of universal or hazardous waste regulations and pursue enforcement action if         21
            necessary. Additionally, I encourage the General Assembly, working with CDPHE, to              22
            consider reforms to this legislation to ensure that the obligation it imposes on propulsion 23
            battery providers and remanufacturers to collect unwanted batteries is conditioned on          24
            secondary handlers abiding by established local, state, and federal waste handling laws.       25
            As passed, the obligation to collect unwanted batteries exists regardless of how a             26
            secondary handler manages propulsion batteries in their possession, potentially exposing 27
            propulsion battery providers and remanufacturers to significant safety and liability risks. 28
                                                                                                           29
            Since this bill gives a new responsibility to propulsion battery providers in collecting and 30
            managing waste at the state level, it is also important that there is no regulatory confusion 31
            between the state and federal level. It is essential that this legislation does not subject    32
            propulsion batte1y providers, remanufacturers and secondary handlers to conflicting rules, 33
            particularly to the degree a propulsion battery is deemed hazardous waste under federal        34
            law. Colorado is already required to ensure its hazardous waste regulations are consistent 35
            with, or more stringent than, federal law. As the bill mandates, CDPHE must determine          36
            next steps if federal laws are enacted around propulsion batteries that impact the             37
            requirements of this bill. I encourage CDP HE, the General Assembly, commercial entities 38
            subject to this bill, and the public to remain active and identify any conflicts with federal 39
            law, existing or new, and take steps to reconcile any such conflicts.                          40
                                                                                                           41
            I appreciate the extensive stakeholder work that went into this bill with the sponsors,        42
            environmental organizations, auto manufacturers, vehicle scrappers, waste haulers and          43
            battery recyclers, and I encourage the General Assembly to evaluate its effectiveness over 44
            time at achieving its intent and to avoid any reduction in EV purchases. I want Colorado 45
            to continue to be a leader in EV adoption and I appreciate that with EV adoption comes         46
            the need to responsibly manage propulsion batteries. This law is the first of its kind in the 47
            nation, and we will learn more as it is implemented and other states start to tackle this      48
            issue.                                                                                         49
                                                                                                           50
               Sincerely,                                                                                  51
               (signed)                                                                                    52
               Jared Polis                                                                                 53
               Governor                                                                                    54
               State of Colorado                                                                           55

            Denver, CO 80203                                                                               66
                                                                                                           67
            Dear Honorable Members of the Colorado State Senate,                                           68
                                                                                                           69
            Today I signed into law Senate Bill 26-006 (SB26-006), "Parity for Non-Opioid Pain             70
            Management Drugs." SB26-006 requires that individual, small group, and large group             71
            health plans provide coverage for at least one non-opioid prescription drug that is            72
Senate Journal-Addendum                                                              Page 1293


available as a clinically appropriate alternative for an opioid. In addition, the cost sharing     1
and utilization management for a non-opioid drug prescribed for the treatment of chronic           2
or acute pain can be no greater or more restrictive than that for opioids.                         3
                                                                                                   4
I am signing this bill today because it represents a small, but meaningful, step towards           5
reducing opioid use in Colorado. The opioid epidemic is far from over in our State: the            6
latest data indicate that overdose deaths increased by 13% in 2025.1 Opioid alternatives           7
can be particularly helpful for people who need pain relief but cannot or will not take            8
opioids, such as those with a past history of substance use disorder. Suzetrigine is one           9
such drug that was discussed during the General Assembly's deliberations, but carriers            10
could satisfy the coverage mandate in SB-006's by covering other clinically appropriate           11
alternatives such as prescription-strength nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), 12
topical pain relievers, medications for nerve pain, or perhaps someday medical marijuana 13
or other fonns of natural medicine. SB26-006 will expand access to these important drugs, 14
and I hope it soon begins to change the trajectory of the opioid epidemic in our State.           15
                                                                                                  16
While I am signing this bill today, I have a concern that drug manufacturers may use a            17
slightly differently worded model of similar legislation in the future to mandate expanded 18
coverage of specific prescription drugs. Coloradans already spend far too much money on 19
prescription drugs: more than half of Coloradans are somewhat or very worried about               20
affording prescription drugs,2 and per-capita spending on prescription drugs nationally           21
increased more than sevenfold between 1980 and 2018, even after adjusting for inflation.3 22
This cannot continue. Rather than advocating for special legislation to account for the cost 23
of their drug, drug companies should adjust their prices to account for the constraints of        24
the marketplace.                                                                                  25
                                                                                                  26
I am also concerned by the precedent set by the cost sharing and utilization management 27
provisions of this bill. The bill effectively eliminates carriers' ability to control utilization 28
of, and reduce costs associated with,. such an expensive drug. The average cost per script 29
of one opioid alternative is approximately $154, but this bill would prohibit cost sharing 30
exceeding that of opioids - which are, on average, less than a quarter of the cost. These         31
sorts of policies tie the hands of entities who might put downward pressure on prices, and 32
clear the way for drug manufacturers to increase costs for Coloradans.                            33
                                                                                                  34
I am signing this bill today because I hope to see continued innovation in this space,            35
including the development of other novel therapies that can provide effective alternatives 36
to opioids. Too many people continue to struggle with opioid use disorder, and we should 37
ensure that patients have every tool available to them to manage pain relief safely -             38
whether it be an opioid alternative approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration or 39
a natural alternative. That's why I signed SB19-013, "Medical Marijuana Condition                 40
Opiates Prescribed For Disabling Medical Conditions," at the beginning of my                      41
administration. It's also part of the reason our regulated Natural Medicine program exists 42
today and why the legislature additionally passed HB26-1325, "Natural Medicine" this              43
year.                                                                                             44
                                                                                                  45
In sum, I am excited about this bill's potential to improve the health of Coloradans.             46
Despite concerns about precedent, it is a critical step towards making Colorado the               47
healthiest state in the nation.                                                                   48
                                                                                                  49
   Sincerely,                                                                                     50
   (signed)                                                                                       51
   Jared Polis                                                                                    52

Dear Honorable Members of the Colorado Senate,                                                    71
                                                                                                  72
Page 1294   Senate Journal-Addendum


            Today, I vetoed Senate Bill 26-184 (SB 26-184), "Firefighter Cancer Benefits & Workers'            1
            Compensation," at 1:30 pm.                                                                         2
                                                                                                               3
            This legislation alters provisions specific to firefighters in the Colorado's Workers'             4
            Compensation program. For firefightets not employed by the State of Colorado, it adds to 5
            the list of cancers considered occupational diseases, and modifies the longstanding                6
            rebuttable presumption by requiring employers to show clear and convincing evidence,               7
            rather than a preponderance of the evidence, that the disease did not occur on the job. It         8
            also diminishes the incentive for fire districts to participate in the Colorado Firefighter        9
            Trust.                                                                                            10
                                                                                                              11
            Firefighters play an extraordinarily important role in our State, from fighting wildfires, to 12
            looking out for our most vulnerable neighbors, to protecting life and property under              13
            highly dangerous circumstances. We are extremely grateful for their service. I have been 14
            asked to veto this bill by the Fire Chiefs, local governments ranging in size from Colorado 15
            Springs to Norwood, and special districts, because it would diminish the durability of the 16
            Colorado Firefighter Trust and puts state employed firefighters on unequal ground with            17
            local firefighters.                                                                               18
                                                                                                              19
            Firefighters face very real short- and long-term health risks. As a result of repeated            20
            exposure to smoke and toxic substances, firefighters face disproportionate rates of several 21
            cancers. For this reason, Colorado's Workers' Compensation program has long treated               22
            firefighters uniquely. Our current system - unique in the country - takes claims out of           23
            workers' compensation and leverages the Colorado Firefighter Trust, which is tailored to 24
            firefighters' needs and expedites claims. It is not perfect, and as I will discuss may be in      25
            need of additional attention, but it is intended to meet the needs firefighters face.             26
                                                                                                              27
            This system is the product of twenty years of work. House Bill 07-1088 established a              28
            rebuttable presumption that certain types of cancer, when contracted by firefighters, are         29
            occupational diseases caused by employment as a firefighter. Unfortunately, this                  30
            presumption, while appropriate, also generated significant litigation and ultimately              31
            delayed benefits for firefighters. To address this issue, Senate Bill 17-214 allowed              32
            employers of firefighters to participate in a voluntary firefighter cancer benefits program 33
            to provide benefits to firefighters, the Colorado Firefighter Trust. As recently as two years 34
            ago under House Bill 24-1219, the General Assembly made a significant investment to               35
            facilitate participation in the Trust. The Trust provides expedited access to benefits,           36
            allows for new cancers to be added outside of the legislative process, and requires no            37
            proof that the cancer is work-related. Under the Trust, the vast majority of claims are           38
            approved sooner, more predictably, and with less litigation. In my meeting with                   39
            firefighters, they rightly pointed out that unfortunately, not all fire districts participate in 40
            the Trust, and I strongly encourage all fire districts to participate in the Trust while          41
            working collaboratively to improve the Trust and address shortcomings.                            42
                                                                                                              43
            Unfortunately, while well-intended, this bill will in fact make it less likely that fire          44
            districts participate in the Trust by removing the incentive for fire districts to participate. I 45
            agree with Fire Chiefs across the State that after Colorado's significant progress on this        46
            issue in recent years, discouraging participation in the Trust would be a step in the wrong 47
            direction for firefighters and fire districts alike. Decreased participation in the Trust might 48
            make it harder for those who do participate to receive the expedited access to benefits and 49
            services they deserve. It will also both raise costs for fire districts and delay benefits to     50
            firefighters. Raising costs for fire districts is also problematic at a time when we need         51
            every resource possible to help with fire preparedness and response.                              52
                                                                                                              53
            Finally, I am deeply concerned that the over 200 firefighters employed by the State of            54
            Colorado were excluded from this legislation after it was introduced, and excluded simply 55
            to avoid a fiscal note. Our State firefighters should not be treated differently than any         56
            other firefighter, as they face many of the same health-related risks. This creates               57
            fundamental fairness issues for State firefighters, and as an employer would make it              58
            harder for the State to hire. I also object to the General Assembly adding these costs for        59
            local fire districts but not to the State.                                                        60
                                                                                                              61
            It is precisely because we value the service of firefighters and recognize the unique health 62
            risks they face that I am vetoing this bill. Going forward, I would encourage further             63
            dialogue between firefighters, fire districts and other local governments, workers'               64
            compensation stakeholders, and other interested parties on what is and is not working for 65
            firefighters in Colorado's existing Workers' Compensation program through a process that 66
            allows for more time for discussions than was provided with this bill. This dialogue              67
            should examine key issues raised by proponents, including nonparticipation in the Trust, 68
            benefit levels, and which cancers it covers. I request an update on these conversations,          69
            including from the Colorado Association of Professional Firefighters and Colorado                 70
            Association of Fire Chiefs, by September 1, 2026, and would encourage those                       71
            conversations to occur to inform legislation should it be necessary next year.                    72
Senate Journal-Addendum                                                             Page 1295


We should do everything we can to ensure that the system works well for these heroes.             1
However, this bill takes us in the wrong direction.                                               2
                                                                                                  3
For these reasons, SB 26-184 is disapproved and vetoed.                                           4
                                                                                                  5
   Sincerely,                                                                                     6
   (signed)                                                                                       7
   Jared Polis                                                                                    8
   Governor                                                                                       9
   State of Colorado                                                                             10

Dear Honorable Members of the Colorado State Senate,                                             23
                                                                                                 24
Today, I vetoed Senate Bill 26-134 (SB 26-134), "Payment Card Networks' Fees," at                25
4:15 pm.                                                                                         26
                                                                                                 27
This bill prohibits a payment card network from charging an interchange fee on the               28
amount of a transaction attributable to tax. The bill aims to exempt cards from issuers that 29
hold assets of less than $60 billion. The bill also requires that a retail business with more 30
than 500 statewide employees applies any savings resulting from the bill to reducing             31
prices for consumers or investing in employee wages or benefits.                                 32
                                                                                                 33
Since similar legislation first came up last year, I have been open to the core concept in       34
this bill and the problem it is trying to solve. Colorado restaurants are the best in the world 35
- and I want to do everything I can to support them during challenging times.                    36
Additionally, the credit card industry is ripe for disruption, and there is far too much         37
friction in our transaction ecosystem. I would support addressing these issues at a national 38
level, while at the state level we should facilitate new financial technologies that provide 39
consumers and businesses with better and more innovative financial products.                     40
                                                                                                 41
Any support we can provide to Colorado's thriving small businesses is worthwhile and             42
should continue to be a priority at the legislature. I want to thank the sponsors for this       43
legislation, and in particular, Senator William Lindstedt, who worked on this bill               44
extraordinarily hard. Their dedication to our small businesses, and in particular our bars       45
and restaurants, is admirable and I deeply appreciate their efforts.                             46
                                                                                                 47
Ultimately, the bill presents too much legal risk to Colorado's business environment and 48
consumers, with limited upside for our small businesses, for me to be comfortable signing. 49
                                                                                                 50
I strongly support Colorado small businesses, especially our restaurant industry, and            51
believe strongly that reducing or eliminating unnecessary fees is important to help small 52
businesses thrive. During my Administration, we have worked to make Colorado the best 53
place to run a small business, including through tax and fiscal policy I have championed 54
that provides relief to small business, initiatives including the Colorado Startup Loan          55
Fund, CLIMBER program, Rural Jump-Start Program, employee ownership supports, and 56
more. We have also placed a special focus on the restaurant community, including this            57
legislative session when my Administration successfully ensured that restaurants would           58
receive tax relief in House Bill 26-1223, "Modifying Certain Tax Expenditures." That bill 59
expands an existing sales tax exemption on energy costs to a full reduction of sales tax         60
paid on energy beginning on January 1, 2026 and re-establishes sales tax retention               61
measures that lets restaurants keep a portion of the sales tax they collect during peak          62
months in 2027 and 2028, with an estimated $1,600 in savings per year in 2027 and 2028 63
from the sales tax deduction and additional savings on utilities bills. These measures           64
provide clear and implementable relief that business owners can count on.                        65
                                                                                                 66
Based on a combined average sales tax of roughly 8%, SB 26-134 - if it ever went into            67
effect - would save merchants roughly 0.13% of the gross total of a purchase. Other              68
policies could provide and more better-targeted relief without the substantial legal risks       69
and delayed timeline this bill entails.                                                          70
                                                                                                 71
First, it is quite possible this bill would never go into effect. Illinois, the only other state 72
Page 1296   Senate Journal-Addendum


            that has passed legislation, passed the similar "Interchange Fee Prohibition Act" (IFPA) as 1
            part of HB495 l I in 2024; more than two years later, implementation of the bill has been      2
            delayed and the bill has been tied up in litigation. After Colorado's own 2026 legislative     3
            session concluded, the Illinois General Assembly again opted to delay implementation of        4
            their legislation for the second time. Additionally, the federal Office of the Comptroller of 5
            the Currency (OCC) and National Credit Union Administration (NCUA) have taken steps 6
            to make clear that the federal government will argue that state-level legislation regarding    7
            swipe fees is preempted by federal law, with the OCC issuing interim final rules and an        8
            order on April 292 and the NCUA more recently indicated it would take action. Just earlier 9
            this week, the U.S. District Court granted a permanent injunction preventing Illinois from 10
            enforcing IFPA's interchange fee limitation against national banks, banks chartered by        11
            states other than Illinois, federal savings associations, and payment card networks. The      12
            ongoing legal and legislative developments of lFPA create unstable grounds for passage 13
            and implementation of SB 26-134 in Colorado.                                                  14
                                                                                                          15
            Even if the bill were to survive legal scrutiny and go into effect in our state, it is        16
            questionable whether this bill is fully implementable or operationally feasible. This would 17
            be a Colorado-specific carve-out to the national and global integrated payments system        18
            and it is unclear to me how the state would implement it. There are a range of possible       19
            outcomes, including potentially requiring consumers to swipe twice for the same               20
            transaction and requiring small businesses to update their payment systems. Worse             21
            outcomes could impact mileage and points cards, tourism, and possibly the availability of 22
            credit or financing products. This could create chaos for our business environment, our       23
            tourism-dependent economy, and consumers that want to make purchases easily and               24
            efficiently.                                                                                  25
                                                                                                          26
            I appreciate that sponsors intended to carve out small- and medium-sized banks and credit 27
            unions from the bill. However, small community banks and credit unions themselves told 28
            my office that, given the integrated nature of the global payments system and partnerships 29
            that exist in practice, they would in practice not be exempt.                                 30
                                                                                                          31
            While not core to the bill, I was also concerned by a Senate floor amendment to require       32
            that a retail business with more than 500 statewide employees apply savings from the bill 33
            in specific ways. This amendment is problematic as a matter of policy. I do not believe it 34
            is appropriate for the government to direct private entities - no matter their size - how to 35
            use their revenues. This provision would also be impossible to enforce and sets a             36
            dangerous precedent in state statute.                                                         37
                                                                                                          38
            I reiterate my thanks to the sponsors for bringing forward this important conversation, but 39
            for the reasons previously stated, I am unable to sign this legislation.                      40
                                                                                                          41
            For these reasons, SB 26-134 is disapproved and vetoed.                                       42
                                                                                                          43
               Sincerely,                                                                                 44
               (signed)                                                                                   45
               Jared Polis                                                                                46
               Governor                                                                                   47

            Dear Honorable Members of the Colorado State Senate,                                          65
                                                                                                          66
            Today, I vetoed Senate Bill 26-005 (SB 26-005), "Rights Violation in Immigration              67
            Enforcement Remedy," at 4:45 pm.                                                              68
                                                                                                          69
            SB 26-005 creates a statutory, civil cause of action specifically and only for Coloradans     70
            whose constitutional rights are violated during a civil immigration enforcement action by 71
            any person acting under the color of any federal, state, or local law. The law is designed to 72
Senate Journal-Addendum                                                         Page 1297


hold local, state, and federal actors accountable during civil immigration enforcement        1
actions.                                                                                      2
                                                                                              3
Let me be clear: no one is above the law. I am keenly aware that current state and federal    4
law allows Coloradans to hold local and state government officials accountable, including 5
law enforcement, for any constitutional violations, while our federal counterparts are not    6
held to the same standard. We have seen too many examples of senseless deaths and             7
constitutional rights violations during immigration enforcement operations and raids in       8
recent years, and there is an urgent need for federal immigration agents to be held           9
accountable for these lawless actions.                                                       10
                                                                                             11
In addition, we have seen other highly visible constitutional violations and threatened      12
violations in other contexts, including free speech and equal protection, in the workplace, 13
elections, schools, and prisons, to name a few. If the federal government won't hold         14
federal officials accountable for violating constitutional rights, then state and local      15
governments must for all violations of our constitutional rights. I applaud the sponsors of 16
this legislation for tackling this critical issue.                                           17
                                                                                             18
Unfortunately, after careful consideration, I believe the legal risks of the actual language 19
in SB 26-005 outweigh the potential benefits. If struck down by a court, it could weaken 20
current protections for vulnerable community members. This concern stems from the bill's 21
narrow focus on civil immigration enforcement - the only circumstances under which           22
constitutional rights are protected by SB 26-005. This bill doesn't apply to any other       23
context besides civil immigration enforcement - including rights violations in protests,     24
elections, prisons, or the workplace. For example, even in the narrow context of             25
immigration, the bill doesn't cover violations of constitutional rights during criminal      26
investigations in immigration. A person whose Fourth or Fifth Amendment rights are           27
violated during a criminal immigration enforcement action should hold the very same          28
remedy as someone whose rights are violated during civil immigration enforcement. It's       29
that narrow focus that unfortunately creates legal jeopardy. I believe Colorado has a        30
chance to get this right - and we must pass a broader version of this bill that protects all 31
constitutional rights, including in the immigration context, that will serve to truly hold   32
public officials accountable.                                                                33
                                                                                             34
During the legislative session, the same sponsors of SB 26-005 worked with my office on 35
Senate Bill 26-176 (SB 26-176), "State Remedies for Constitutional Rights Violation," an 36
alternative to SB 26-005 that took a more expansive approach to accountability - one that 37
my office believed would withstand legal scrutiny, and which would have provided             38
protections for Coloradans against all manner of constitutional violation by federal agents. 39
The very purpose of a Universal Constitutional Remedies Act (UCRA) is to provide a           40
remedy for any constitutional rights violations occurring under color of law. This is        41
precisely the remedy that SB 26-176 sought to provide. SB 26-176, and UCRA legislation 42
across the country, follows in the historic tradition and courage of those lawmakers who 43
stood firm in the face of the vitriol advanced by the Ku Klux Klan and who passed 42         44
U.S.C. Section 1983, which holds state and local officials accountable for violations of     45
the U.S. Constitution.                                                                       46
                                                                                             47
Unfortunately, and despite the sponsors' admirable and tireless work to move that bill       48
forward, it died in the process due to overly intense and misleading lobbying from local     49
governments and public entities. For example, those entities indicated that state courts     50
could not handle complex constitutional rights cases, which I believe is not true.           51
Long-standing federal law already establishes liability for state and local officials for    52
constitutional rights violations, and courts in our state decide these cases regularly.1 If  53
Colorado would have passed that bill, we would have joined a growing list of states that 54
are choosing to defend against all constitutional violations, including California, Maine, 55
Massachusetts, and New Jersey, who have had legislation for more than 20 years, as well 56
as Connecticut, New York, Maryland, Rhode Island, and Vermont who have introduced 57
or passed this type of legislation in the last two years. Coloradans deserve the same        58
protections for their constitutional rights as our sister states, and local governments and  59
political subdivisions should be willing to learn from the experience of those states where 60
these issues have been and are being debated.                                                61
                                                                                             62
I firmly believe that constitutional rights should be protected in all contexts, and for all 63
persons. Thats not only a good policy I completely agree with, and puts us on strong legal 64
footing. Constitutional rights are a shield against government overreach and misconduct; 65
they are vital to any democracy, and especially to our own at this time. It defies the very  66
purpose of natural rights if they are only available when the circumstances, set by one      67
legislature, are just right.                                                                 68
                                                                                             69
I want to thank the sponsors for their leadership in bringing forward one of the most        70
critical debates of our time, both in the form of SB 26-005 and SB 26-17 6, especially       71
knowing how much pushback SB 26-176 received. Looking forward, I strongly                    72
Page 1298   Senate Journal-Addendum


            encourage all stakeholders who engaged in these discussions to continue conversations to 1
            find a solution to protect constitutional rights beyond only the civil immigration             2
            enforcement context and to work towards a solution similar to SB 26-176. Colorado              3
            stands finn in its belief that constitutional rights violations deserve an adequate deterrent  4
            and remedy, and any legislation purporting to provide both should apply to all contexts. In 5
            the coming months, I will be working with all stakeholders to engage in this debate going 6
            forward.                                                                                       7
                                                                                                           8
            It is important to provide a workable remedy that is on the best legal footing and gives       9
            Coloradans a meaningful opportunity to seek justice against government agents who             10
            commit constitutional violations.                                                             11
                                                                                                          12
            For these reasons, SB 26-005 is disapproved and vetoed.                                       13
                                                                                                          14
                Sincerely,                                                                                15
                (signed)                                                                                  16
                Jared Polis                                                                               17
                Governor                                                                                  18
                State of Colorado                                                                         19

                 CHANGE IN MEMBERSHIP

                         SENATE
                 75th GENERAL ASSEMBLY




                           Adrienne Benavidez



On Monday, March 2, 2026, Adrienne Benavidez, of Commerce City,
was sworn in to the Seventy-fifth General Assembly as Senator for
Senate District 21, to fill the vacancy created by the resignation of Senator
Dafna Michaelson Jenet. Colorado Court of Appeals Justice Lino S.
Lipinsky de Orlov administered the oath of office in the Chamber of the
Senate.
